en: Śrī Parīkṣit said:
The path of renunciation has been described by Your Lordship at the outset, wherein non-return to saṃsāra is attained through Brahman reached by gradual yoga.

O Sage, you have described the path of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), which is characterized by the three *guṇas* and pertains to the realm of the *guṇas*, as well as that creation of the *guṇas* which occurs again and again for one whose nature has not been dissolved; and you have also described the various hells characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*).
The first Manvantara, that of Svāyambhuva, has been explained,
as well as the lineages and deeds of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda,
along with the continents, regions, oceans, mountains, rivers, gardens, and trees.

O highly fortunate one, just as the All-pervading Lord formerly created this configuration of the terrestrial sphere— including its divisions, characteristics, and measurements— as well as the celestial bodies and the subterranean cavities, so now [describe] here how a man [falls into] the hells.
"May he not go to those various fierce hells; you ought to explain that to me.
Śrī Śuka said:
"If one does not perform atonement here in this very life for the sin committed, according to the words of Manu, by means of penance, recitation, or ritual offerings,"

"Indeed, after death, he shall surely enter those hells of sharp torments that I have described to you. Therefore, even before death, one should strive here for the expiation of sin with a self that is not subject to failure;
just as a physician who knows the causes of disease treats an ailment after having observed its severity or mildness."
The King said:

"Even though one knows that a certain action is harmful to oneself—whether through seeing or hearing it—is it not the case that, being helpless, one performs it again and again? What then is the atonement for such an act?"
"In one case he turns away from evil, and in another he engages in it again;
therefore, I consider such atonement to be as useless as the bathing of an elephant.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
The removal of karma through karma is not considered to be ultimate, because it is prescribed for those who lack true knowledge; rather, the investigation of atonement is required.
For just as diseases overcome one who does not eat wholesome food, so too do they prevail over one who lacks discernment.
O King, one who thus observes these restraints gradually becomes fit for security through austerity, celibacy, tranquility, self-control,
renunciation, truthfulness, purity, restraint, and observance.

The wise, who know the dharma and are endowed with faith, cast off even great evil born of body, speech, and mind, just as fire consumes a thicket of bamboo. Some, devoted solely to Vāsudeva through pure devotion alone, [attain the same].

They shake off their sins entirely, just as the sun dispels the mist. O King, a person burdened by sin is not purified by austerities and the like in the same way that one whose life is surrendered to Kṛṣṇa is purified by serving His devotees.
For this is the path in this world that leads directly to well-being and is free from fear from any quarter— the path where the virtuous and saintly ones, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
abide. Yet, penances performed for one who is averse to Nārāyaṇa [bear no fruit].

O King of kings, those whose minds have been placed even once here upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa and who are enamored of His qualities do not purify [their minds] again, just as rivers do not flow back into a jar of liquor;
indeed, having performed their atonement, they do not see Yama, his messengers, or his guards even in a dream.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
learn from me the conversation between the messengers of Viṣṇu and Yama.
In Kānyakubja, there was a certain twice-born man named Ajāmila, who was the husband of a maidservant.

By name [he was] Naṣṭasadācāra; corrupted by association with a slave woman, he adopted a despicable livelihood through gambling, deception, and theft. Being impure, he maintained a family and tormented embodied beings.
O King, as he lived in this manner, fondling his sons,
eighty-eight years of his life passed away.
Of those ten sons of his who had reached old age, the youngest was...
Named Nārāyaṇa, he was a child who was dearly beloved by his parents. With his heart bound to that infant who spoke with the sweet voice of a young elephant,
the aged king took great delight as he gazed upon the child’s playful activities.

Eating, drinking, and chewing, constrained by affection for his child, the fool— while feeding and nursing him— does not perceive that death has arrived. Thus conducting himself, the ignorant man finds the time of death standing before him.
He set his mind upon his young son, named Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing three extremely fierce men with nooses in their hands,
crooked snouts, and bristling hair, who had arrived to take him away, he [was struck with fear].
With his senses agitated, he called out in a loud, choked voice to his son named Nārāyaṇa, who was playing with toys far away,
having heard from the mouth of one dying the glorification of Hari.
O great king, as soon as they heard their master’s name, the attendants suddenly descended from within his heart, dragging out Ajāmila, the husband of slave-girls;
then the messengers of Viṣṇu forcibly warded off the servants of Yama.
Being thus forbidden by them, those who were at the forefront of Vaivasvata’s retinue said:
"Who are you that prohibit the command of Dharmarāja?
Whom do you belong to, from where have you come, and for what reason do you forbid him?"
"Are you gods or secondary deities, or perhaps the most excellent of the Siddhas? For all of you have eyes like lotus petals, wear saffron silk garments,
and are adorned with crowns, earrings, and shimmering garlands of lotuses."
All of them possessed fresh youth, and all had beautiful four arms; they were adorned with the splendor of bows, quivers, swords, maces, conchs, discs, and lotuses,
illuminating the quarters with their own luster and dispelling the darkness.
"For what purpose do you restrain us, the servants of Dharmapāla?
Śrī Śuka said:
When they had been addressed thus by the messengers of Yama, those who carry out the commands of Vāsudeva...
Laughing, the messengers of Śrī Viṣṇu replied to them with voices as deep as the roar of clouds: The messengers of Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"If you are indeed the executors of the commands of Dharmarāja..."
"Tell us the true nature of dharma and the characteristics of adharma;
how indeed is the rod of punishment wielded, and what is its desired locus?
Are all offenders subject to punishment, or only some among men?"
The messengers of Yama said:
"Dharma is that which is enjoined by the Veda, while adharma is its opposite.
We have heard that the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the self-existent."
By whom these entities, composed of the qualities of passion, goodness, and ignorance, are manifested within His own abode according to their true nature through names, functions, and forms—
He is the sun, fire, ether, wind, the gods, the moon, twilight, day and night, and the directions.
"Kaṃsa, Ku, and Dharma himself—these are indeed the witnesses of the embodied soul.
When unrighteousness is recognized by these, it is appropriate that punishment be meted out. All perpetrators deserve punishment in accordance with their actions."
O sinless ones, auspicious and adverse results indeed arise for those who act; for one who possesses a body, there is attachment to the qualities of action, for no one is without action.
Whatever dharma or adharma has been performed here by anyone, to whatever extent, and in whatever manner— [it bears fruit accordingly].
He alone experiences that fruit in the hereafter for exactly as long as it lasts,
just as the threefold variety is perceived here among the foremost of the gods due to the diversity of qualities in living beings; so too is it inferred elsewhere.
Just as the present time makes known the qualities of the other two [past and future],
so too does this birth reveal the righteousness and unrighteousness of the other two births;
by the mind alone, O Lord, the deity perceives his former form within the city of the body.

The unborn Lord, with his mind, deliberated upon that unprecedented matter; for just as one who is ignorant and shrouded in darkness perceives only the manifest, so too he did not know what was before or what was after, having lost the memory of his previous births.
With five [senses] it performs its own purposes, and with another five it experiences the five objects;
the one [mind], however, through the sixteenth [element], enjoys the three [qualities], while itself being the seventeenth.
This very subtle body (*liṅga*) consists of sixteen parts and possesses the three great powers (*śakti*).
It causes the individual soul to undergo the cycle of rebirth, which brings joy, grief, fear, and suffering.
O embodied one, the ignorant person, unable to conquer the six internal enemies, is driven by actions against his will;
like a silkworm, he deludes himself by enveloping himself with his own karma.

Indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action; for, being powerless, one is driven by force by actions born of one's own inherent qualities (guṇas). Having obtained the unmanifest cause, it indeed becomes manifest and unmanifest.

Just as [the seed] corresponds to its womb and its own seed, so too, through the power of inherent nature (svabhāva), this perversion of the person (puruṣa) occurs due to attachment to material nature (prakṛti). That very [perversion] dissolves before long through union with the Lord (īśa).
For he is endowed with sacred learning, a repository of good conduct, observance, and virtue;
firm in his vows, gentle, self-controlled, truthful in speech, skilled in mantras, and pure;
devoted to serving his guru, the sacrificial fire, guests, and elders, and free from egoism.
A virtuous man, a friend to all beings, moderate in speech, and free from envy—
that twice-born one, carrying out his father’s command, once went to the forest;
having taken fruits, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass, he returned from there.
He saw a certain lustful Śūdra together with his female slave;
having drunk maireya liquor, she was intoxicated, her eyes rolling from the intoxication,
her waist-knot loosened, and she was shameless.
Seeing her playing, singing along, and laughing near him, and seeing her embraced by his arm— an arm smeared with passion—
he suddenly fell under the sway of lust, utterly bewildered.

Stiffening himself by his own will as much as possible according to what he had heard, he was nevertheless unable to compose his mind, which was trembling with passion; seized by the demon of Smara (Love) under that pretext, he became unconscious.
Meditating upon her alone with his mind, he indeed desisted from his own duty;
he gratified her with as much ancestral wealth as was necessary, and with such delightful worldly pleasures as would cause her to be pleased.
That wicked man, his mind pierced by the sidelong glances of a wanton woman, soon abandoned his own young wife, a Brahmin lady born into a great family; meanwhile,
he procured wealth from here and there, both by lawful and unlawful means.
This dull-witted man supported the family of his wife because he had transgressed the scriptures and acted according to his own whims; being exceedingly contemptible,
impure, and foul due to his sins, he lived for a long time as one whose life was dedicated to evil.
"Therefore, we shall lead this man, who has committed an offense and has not yet performed atonement, into the presence of Daṇḍapāṇi, where he may be purified by means of punishment.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
O King, having thus understood what was spoken by the messengers of Yama, those messengers of the Blessed One, who were experts in policy, replied to them. The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Unrighteousness touches the assembly of those who perceive the Dharma, wherein punishment is wielded in vain against those who are unworthy of it and free from sin.
For they are the fathers of the subjects, their instructors, the virtuous, and impartial."
If there were indeed inequality among them, to whom would living beings go for refuge?
Whatever a superior person practices, others strive to do that;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
How could he— who, placing his head upon [Viṣṇu’s] lap, sleeps peacefully,
being himself like a beast that knows neither dharma nor adharma—
abandon one who has surrendered his soul and established friendship with him, even if that one were unconscious?
One who is trustworthy toward all beings and compassionate deserves to milk [the earth];
for he has already expiated the sins of ten million births by involuntarily uttering the name of Hari, which is a source of auspiciousness.
By this alone, the expiation for the sins of this sinner would be accomplished,
when he uttered the four syllables "Nārāyaṇāya.
A thief, a drinker of liquor, a betrayer of friends, a slayer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the teacher’s bed— [by this, all their sins are removed].
For those who have killed a woman, a king, their father, or a cow, and for all other sinners as well,
this alone is the perfect atonement for their transgressions:
the utterance of Viṣṇu’s name, since that is the means by which the mind becomes fixed upon Him.

A sinner is not purified by the expiatory rites prescribed by the exponents of the Veda, nor by vows and other such observances, in the same way that he is purified by the utterance of the names of Hari, which bring about the realization of the qualities of Him whose fame is supreme. For even when an expiation has been performed, the mind may yet run back onto the path of unrighteousness; thus, that purification is not absolute.

For those who desire the removal of their karma, the chanting of the qualities of Hari is indeed the purifier of the mind. Therefore, do not lead him away; he has performed the expiation for all his sins, since he grasped the name of the Blessed One while dying.
Whether uttered as a sign, in jest, as a chant, or even in derision,
they know that the utterance of the name of Vaikuṇṭha removes every sin without exception.
Whether one is fallen, stumbling, broken, bitten, scorched, or struck;
A person who involuntarily utters the name "Hari" does not deserve the torments of hell.
The great sages, having understood the gravity and lightness of sins as well as the gravity and lightness of the offenses, have prescribed heavy and light penances accordingly.
Those sins are purified by austerities, charity, vows, and the like;
yet that heart born of unrighteousness is not [purified] even by that, except through service to the feet of the Lord.
Whatever [offense] has been committed against the One of Excellent Fame, whether out of ignorance or with knowledge—

The chanting of his names burns away a person's sins just as fire consumes fuel; and just as a most potent medicine, when taken even by chance, produces its medicinal effect upon the body without the person's knowledge, so too does a mantra produce its result when it is uttered.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus thoroughly determined the Bhāgavata dharma,
they released that brāhmaṇa from the nooses of Yama and liberated him from death.
O subduer of enemies, having been thus addressed, the messengers of Yama departed for the presence of Yama and reported everything exactly as it was to King Yama; meanwhile,
the twice-born man, released from the noose, became free from fear and returned to his natural state.

Feeling the joy of a vision, he bowed his head to the servants of Viṣṇu. O sinless one, perceiving that he wished to speak, those servants of the Great Person suddenly vanished from there while he was looking on.
Then Ajāmila, having heard from the messengers of Yama and Kṛṣṇa about the pure Bhāgavata dharma, which rests upon the three Vedas and the [three] guṇas,
quickly became devoted to the Lord Hari through hearing of His majesty.
Great was his remorse as he recalled his own evil deed:
"Alas! For me, who had failed to conquer my self, a supreme misery has occurred; by which I, having violated the Veda, have caused myself to be born from a Śūdra woman."
"Fie on me, censured by the virtuous, a doer of evil who stains my lineage!
For, abandoning my young and chaste wife, I have gone to an unchaste woman who drinks liquor. My aged parents are without other protectors; they are wretched and have no kin but me."
"Alas! Having now abandoned [them], I, ungrateful as a base person, shall clearly fall into a most dreadful hell,
where those who destroy dharma and are full of lust undergo the torments of Yama."
“Is this a dream, or is this a wonderful sight seen here in person? Where have those who dragged me along with nooses in their hands gone today?
And where have those four Siddhas of beautiful appearance gone?”
They released him as he was being led away, bound by ropes beneath the earth;
yet, even for one as unfortunate as I, there must have been some auspicious destiny in beholding the best of the gods, by which my soul finds peace.

Otherwise, how could the tongue of one who is dying—impure and the husband of a low-caste woman—be capable of uttering the name of Vaikuṇṭha? And where am I: a gambler, a sinner, a slayer of Brahmins, and utterly shameless?
And where is this auspicious name of the Blessed One, "Nārāyaṇa"? Therefore, I shall strive with my mind, senses, and breath restrained, so that I may not again sink my self into blind darkness.
Having liberated himself from this bondage born of ignorance, desire, and karma—
being a friend to all beings, peaceful, friendly, compassionate, and self-possessed—
he shall release his own self, which was swallowed by the illusory power consisting of womanhood.
By her alone was I toyed with like a lowly pet deer;
having abandoned the false-minded notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth,
I shall fix my mind upon the Blessed Lord through the chanting of His glories and other such means.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus become thoroughly disillusioned by his momentary association with the virtuous,
and having abandoned all worldly attachments, he went to Gaṅgādvāra.
Seated there in that divine abode, having established himself in yoga and withdrawn the collection of his senses, he joined his mind to the Self; then,
through self-concentration, he separated the Self from the material qualities.

When his mind was withdrawn from all else and fixed upon the Supreme Lord— the Brahman that is the self of direct experience— the twice-born sage beheld before him the Puruṣas. Having perceived those who had been perceived by him previously, he bowed his head in salutation.

Having cast off his body at the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā immediately after the vision, the brahmin instantly assumed his true form along with the servants of the Great Person, who were standing by the side of the Blessed One, and ascended into the sky.
Ascending a golden celestial chariot, he went to where the Lord of Śrī resides.
Thus, though he had caused all dharma to be swept away and was the husband of a maidservant, that fallen man of censurable deeds—
his vows destroyed and being cast down into hell— was immediately liberated while uttering the name of the Blessed One.
There is nothing superior to the chanting of the names of the Lord whose feet are the source of all holy places for those seeking liberation that cuts through the bonds of karma;
for by such chanting, the mind—which otherwise becomes clouded by passion and ignorance—is no longer attached to worldly activities.
This supreme secret history is the destroyer of sins.
He who listens with faith and he who recites it with devotion shall certainly not go to hell, nor shall he be seen by the servants of Yama;
even if that mortal is inauspicious, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Even Ajāmila, while dying, attained the abode of Hari by chanting His name as it was uttered by his son; how much more so for one who chants it with faith!
Śrī Rājā said:

Having heard what was described by his own soldiers, the god Dharmarāja replied: "What of them as well? They too have been slain by the messengers of Murāri, whose command has thus been thwarted—he under whose control this entire world stands. O sage, has it ever been heard before that there has been any failure of the rod of punishment on the part of the god Yama?"
"O Sage, it is my firm conviction that no one other than you can cut through this doubt of the world.
Śrī Śuka said:
"O King, the messengers of Yama had their efforts thwarted by the servants of the Blessed Lord."
They informed their master, Yama, the lord of Saṃyamanī.
The messengers of Yama said:
"O Lord, how many rulers are there here in the world of the living?"

If there were many teachers wielding the rod of punishment in this world who would ensure that the threefold division of duties is maintained, then for whom would there be the manifestation of the fruits of action,
and for whom would there not? Or rather, for whom would there be death, and for whom immortality?

But when there is a plurality of teachers, the status of being a teacher here belongs to many among those who perform ritual actions; for such a title is merely figurative, as in the case of the rulers of provinces.
Therefore, you alone are the sovereign lord of all beings, including the gods.
You are the teacher and the wielder of the rod for men, the discriminator between good and evil;
yet now, in this world, your ordained punishment does not prevail,
for your command has been subverted by these four wonderful Siddhas.
"By your command, we were leading this sinner away to the houses of torment; you forcibly released him by cutting his bonds.
We wish to know who those people are, if you consider it appropriate for us to know."
When "Nārāyaṇa" was uttered, [the messengers] quickly approached, saying, "Do not fear.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Thus questioned by the god Yama, the restrainer of living beings, he—
Being pleased, he spoke to his messengers while remembering the lotus feet of Hari.
Yama said:
"Other than me, there is no one else who is the Supreme Lord of the moving and the stationary, in whom the entire universe is woven like a cloth."
He from whose portion arise the maintenance, birth, and destruction of this world, and under whose control the universe remains;
he who binds people to his own speech with names, as one binds cattle with ropes to a tethering post;
and whom these people, bound by the fetters of name and ritual action, carry as their sacrificial offering in fear.

I am Mahendra, Nirṛti, Pracetas, Soma, Agni, Īśa, Pavana, and Viriñci; I am the Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the Rudras along with the Siddhas; and I am all other creators of the universe, lords of the immortals, such as Bhṛgu and others, who are untouched by passion and darkness.

Even those whose nature is predominantly *sattva* do not understand His will when it is touched by *māyā*; how much less so others? Indeed, those who bear the vital breaths do not perceive Him with their senses, mind, life-breaths, heart, or speech—Him who, like the eye within the self, dwells as the Self within the hearts of all beings, beyond even that which is unmanifest.

The messengers of that self-dependent Lord Hari, the Supreme Sovereign and Great Soul who masters Māyā, generally wander here in this world possessing forms, qualities, and natures like His own. These beings of Viṣṇu are worshipped by the gods; their manifestations are wondrous and difficult to behold.

They protect mortals who are devoted to Him from others, from me, and from all [dangers]; yet neither the sages, nor the gods, nor the foremost of the Siddhas, nor the Asuras, nor humans know that Dharma directly proclaimed by the Blessed Lord— how then could the Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and others know it?
"O warriors, we twelve— Svayambhū, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, and the son of Vyāsa— know this Bhāgavata Dharma."
This secret, pure, and difficult-to-understand [truth], by knowing which one attains immortality—
this alone is considered the supreme duty for men in this world:
the yoga of devotion toward the Blessed One through the chanting of His names and other such means.
"O sons, behold the greatness of uttering the name of Hari!
Even Ajāmila was liberated from the noose of death by that very act. This alone is sufficient for the removal of the sins of men."
The chanting of the qualities, deeds, and names of the Blessed One—
by which even the sinful Ajāmila, while dying, cried out "Nārāyaṇa" for his son and attained liberation.

Generally, this great multitude does not know this [truth], for alas, their intellects have been utterly deluded by the Goddess’s Māyā; their minds have become dulled by the three Vedas, which are like flowers blooming with honey.
While engaged in great Vedic rituals,
the wise, having reflected thus, indeed apply themselves with their whole being to the yoga of devotion toward the infinite Lord.
They do not deserve punishment from me; moreover, even if they were to commit a sin, the chanting of the names of the Wide-Strider (Urugāya) destroys it.
Their songs of praise are pure, celebrated by gods and perfected beings (siddhas).
Do not approach those saintly persons who look upon all with equality and have taken refuge in the Lord; for they are protected by the mace of Hari,
and neither we nor our power are capable of inflicting punishment upon them.
Bring them here— those who have turned away from the nectar of the lotus feet of Mukunda, which is constantly tasted by the unattached hosts of Paramahaṃsas who possess nothing.
The tongue of one who has developed a thirst for the path to hell while dwelling in the home does not speak the names and qualities of the Blessed One,
nor does the mind remember His lotus feet.
"Bring those wicked ones who do not bow their heads even once to Kṛṣṇa, for they have failed to perform their duty toward Viṣṇu.
May that Blessed One, the Ancient Puruṣa, forgive them."

O Nārāyaṇa, that you have forgiven what was done to us by your own servants— alas, even though we are ignorant and have joined our palms in supplication— to you, the Supreme Person, the Infinite, who possesses such great forbearance toward your own people, I offer my obeisances.

Therefore, O descendant of Kuru, know that the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names— the auspiciousness of the universe— is the singular and absolute atonement even for the great sins of men. This is so for those who repeatedly hear and proclaim the exalted heroic deeds of Hari.
Just as the self is purified by well-born devotion rather than by vows and the like,
so too one who has tasted the honey of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet does not again take pleasure in the qualities of Māyā, which bring only suffering.
But another, struck by desire, strives to wipe away the dust from his own soul, only for that very action to cause the dust to arise once again.
Thus [he heard] the majesty of the Blessed One as spoken by his own master.

O King, having recollected this, those servants of Yama, their minds struck with wonder and fearing that he might be one who has taken refuge in Acyuta, have been afraid to even look at him from that time forward.
The Blessed One, born from a jar (Agastya), while seated on Mount Malaya and worshiping Hari, narrated this secret history. Śrī Rājā said:

You have briefly described the creation of the gods, asuras, humans, nagas, beasts, and birds that occurred during the Svāyambhuva interval; O Blessed One, I desire to know its detailed expansion from you exactly as it was.
"By which power the Supreme Lord created the secondary creation.
Śrī Sūta said:
"Having heard this inquiry from the royal sage, the son of Bādarāyaṇa..."
Having greeted them, the great yogi spoke, O best of sages;
Śrī Śuka said:
"When the ten Pracetasas were the sons of Prācīnabarhis..."
Emerging from within the ocean, they beheld the earth covered with trees;
incensed by those trees and their wrath kindled by ascetic power,
they emitted wind and fire from their mouths, desiring to consume them.
O best of the Kurus, perceiving them being scorched by those two,
King Soma spoke, as if to pacify their wrath:
"O highly fortunate ones, you ought not to bear malice toward these wretched trees."
"You are known as the lords of creatures, intended to cause their increase. Oh, the Lord Hari, the imperishable Master of the Lords of Creatures,
the all-pervading one, created the trees and the herbs for the sake of vigor and nourishment."

The immobile are the food of the mobile; the footless are the food of those who move on feet; the handless are the food of those endowed with hands; and the two-footed are the food of the four-footed. And you, O sinless ones, have been commanded by your father and by the God of gods.

Indeed, for the sake of procreation, how can you deign to burn down the trees? Follow the path of the virtuous; restrain your blazing anger, which has been practiced by your father, grandfather, and great-grandfathers.
He is the parents and kinsmen of children; He is the eyelashes for the eyes of women, and the husband of wives.
He is the master of progeny, the householder of mendicants, and the wise friend of the ignorant.
Within the bodies of all beings, Hari dwells as the Supreme Lord and the Self.
Behold all that splendor, for he has thus been propitiated. Indeed,
he who, through the desire to know the Self, restrains the fierce anger that has arisen within his body like a tempest from the sky, transcends the material qualities (*guṇas*).
"Enough with these wretched, burnt trees; may it be well with you who are barren.
For this excellent maiden of the trees shall be accepted as your wife. Having thus addressed the beautiful maiden, who was like an *apsaras*, O King, [the sage spoke].
King Soma departed after giving her away; they wed her according to dharma.
From them, through her, Dakṣa Prācetasa was born, by whose emission of progeny the three worlds were filled.

Listen attentively as I describe how Dakṣa, who was affectionate toward his daughters, created living beings through both semen and the mind alone. In the beginning, Prajāpati created these creatures by means of the mind alone.

Seeing that the creation of beings— gods, asuras, humans, and others dwelling in the sky, on land, and in water— had increased excessively, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) went to the foothills of the Vindhya mountains and performed difficult austerities.
There, at the supreme holy site named Aghamarṣaṇa, which destroys all sins,
he performed ablutions at each of the three daily junctures and gratified Hari through his ascetic penance;
he praised the Lord Adhokṣaja with the Haṃsa-guhya hymn.
I shall describe that to you, as well as how Hari was pleased with whom. Śrī Prajāpati said:
"Obeisances to the Supreme One, whose experience is unfailing, who is the cause of the appearance of the three modes of nature, and who is the kinsman of those bound by them."

I bow to the Self-born One, whose abode is unseen by those whose intellects perceive the principles of the *guṇas*, and who has withdrawn from the *māna* (ego); to Him with whom no person—though dwelling as a friend within this city [of the body] alongside that Friend—recognizes friendship, just as a quality is not perceived by one who clearly sees the possessor of the quality; to that Great Lord, I offer salutation.
The body, the vital breaths, the senses, the mind, the elements, and the subtle constituents—these know themselves and that which is other than them, the Supreme.
The person knows all this and the qualities thereof; yet, though he is the knower, he does not know the All-Knowing, Infinite One. I praise Him.
When the cessation of the mind occurs due to the loss of the perception and memory of name and form...
Salutations to that Swan, the abode of purity, who moves by his own singular nature.

Just as the wise, through their intelligence, draw forth the hidden fire within wood— composed of fifteen parts and established within the heart by means of the nine and threefold powers— so do they perceive You.
He indeed is the experience of the bliss of liberation, which negates all the specific manifestations of my *māyā*;

He possesses all names and is the universal form; may He, whose self-power is inexpressible, be gracious. Whatever is defined by speech, or determined by the intellect, the senses, or even by the mind—He is that.
Let it not be that His essential nature consists of the modes; rather, that very nature is characterized by the appearance and disappearance of the modes.

That Brahman, which is the supreme among the high and the low, is primordially established as the cause of all; it is the one without a second, from whom, by whom, through whom, for whom, what, who, and in what manner one acts and is acted upon.

Salutations to that Infinite One of boundless qualities, whose powers become the source of dispute and agreement for those who speak and debate, and who repeatedly cause them self-delusion. [Salutations] to Him who,
while abiding as one in the reality of things, possesses both "it exists" and "it does not exist"— attributes that are distinct and contradictory.
Whatever has been observed in Yoga and Sāṅkhya is indeed equal to that supreme, vast,

and favorable reality. May that Supreme Lord, who is without name or form, yet assumes names and forms through His births and activities for the sake of favoring those who worship at the soles of His feet, be gracious unto me.
May that Lord— who, residing within the bodies of living beings, appears according to their inclinations through the paths of material knowledge,
just as the wind manifests its qualities when resting upon the earth— fulfill my heart’s desire.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the Kurus, when he had thus praised him while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared there;
his feet were placed upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, and his eight great arms hung down.
Holding a discus, conch, sword, shield, bow, noose, and mace;
clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, with a serene face and eyes;
his body draped with a forest garland, shining with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem.
Wearing a great crown and bracelets, with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings, and adorned with a girdle, rings, bangles, anklets, and armlets,
the Lord of the three worlds assumed a form that enchants the three worlds.
Surrounded by his attendants, headed by Nārada and Nanda, as well as by the leaders of the hosts of gods,
and being praised and followed by singing Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, [the King],
beholding that most wonderful form, was struck with awe.

With a heart overflowing with joy, Prajāpati prostrated himself on the ground like a staff; he was unable to utter a single word, as his mind and senses were filled by an intense rapture, like a mountain spring filling a lake.
To that Prajāpati, who was thus bowed down in devotion and desiring offspring,
Janārdana— who knows the hearts of all beings— spoke this.
The Blessed Lord said:
O highly fortunate son of Pracetas, you have attained perfection through your austerity,
since by supreme faith directed toward Me, you have reached the highest state of being within Me.
O lord of creatures, I am pleased with you because of this austerity of yours which increases your strength.

This is my desire for all beings: that their prosperity may increase. Brahmā, Śiva, you [the sages], the Manus, and the lords of the gods—these are indeed my manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), the causes of prosperity for all beings.
O Brahmin, austerity is my heart, sacred knowledge is my body, and ritual action is my form; the sacrifices have become my limbs, dharma is my soul, and the gods are my vital breaths.
In the beginning, I alone existed—nothing else whatsoever, neither within nor without.

The unmanifest, which was mere consciousness, lay as if asleep on all sides; from Me, who am infinite and possessed of infinite qualities, there arose by virtue of My qualities that primordial, unborn, and self-existent Being whose form consists of the modes of nature.
When that Mahādeva, empowered by my virility,
prepared for the task of creating heaven, he considered himself as if deficient;
thereupon, the Lord was addressed by me and performed severe austerities.
O lords of progeny, by whom the all-pervading Lord first created you nine creators of the universe—
this daughter of Prajāpati Pañcajana,
named Asiknī, let her be accepted as your wife.

You, whose nature is sexual union, shall again bring forth this creation of progeny in abundance through a female who possesses the nature of sexual union; from you, all beings below shall be produced by means of Māyā through sexual coupling.
"They shall become mine and they shall offer me tribute.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus while he was looking on, the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, [vanished].
Like an object perceived in a dream, Hari vanished right there.
Śrī Śuka said:
Upon that conch-shell [of Pāñcajanya], he was indeed augmented by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
The powerful one begot ten thousand sons known as the Haryaśvas;

O King, all those descendants of Dakṣa were identical in their religious character and conduct. When commanded by their father regarding the creation of progeny, they departed toward the western direction.
There, at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, is the great Nārāyaṇa-saras tīrtha, which is frequented by sages and perfected beings;
merely by bathing there, the impurities of their hearts were completely washed away.
Even though their minds were directed toward the dharma of the paramahaṃsas,
they performed fierce austerities, constrained by the command of their father;
the celestial sage indeed beheld them as they were thus striving for the increase of progeny.
Then the Haryaśvas said: "How indeed will you create progeny when you have not seen the end of the earth? Alas, you are but foolish guardians!
Likewise, there is but one man in the kingdom, and the hole has no visible exit."
He saw a woman of many forms, as well as a man who was the husband of an unchaste woman;
a river flowing in both directions, and a house with twenty-five wonders; in one place, a swan engaged in various stories, and a barber himself wandering about.
"How can you wise ones, not knowing the command of your own father and failing to understand what is appropriate, say, 'Alas, we shall create the world'? Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard that, the sons of Haryaśva,
through their innate intelligence, reflected within themselves upon the cryptic words of the celestial sage:
"The earth is the field, known as the individual soul (jīva), which is beginningless and its own bondage."
Without seeing his liberation, what would be the use of evil deeds?
The Lord alone is the Supreme, the Fourth State (turya), self-abiding and transcendent;
without seeing Him, what would be the use of a person's evil deeds?
Having once gone there, a person never returns, just as one who has entered the subterranean heavens (bilasvarga) does not;
for one who knows the inward abode, what could be gained here by fruitless actions?
The intellect of the self, which assumes various forms, is like a wanton woman attached to the modes of nature.
For one who has not attained steadfastness in that [devotion], what can be achieved here by means of improper actions?

For the ignorant man whose sovereignty is lost through attachment to those [objects] and who wanders in saṃsāra like a wretched wife, what can be achieved here by means of improper actions? What purpose would his courses of action serve?

What can be gained by the wicked deeds of one who is intoxicated and ignorant of that Māyā, which causes both creation and dissolution, and which possesses a speed like the surging tide at the edge of the shore? The Puruṣa is the wondrous mirror for the twenty-five principles.
For one who is ignorant of the supreme self in this world, what can be achieved by improper actions?
Having cast aside the scripture concerning the Lord, which reveals both bondage and liberation,
and failing to understand the state of solitude, what can be achieved by improper actions?
The wheel of time revolves with sharp edges, dragging away the entire world.
For one who is not enlightened, what can be achieved here by independent and improper actions?
He who does not know the instruction of the father-like scripture which brings about cessation [of worldly existence].

"O King, how may we approach him who is worthy of us and who places his trust in our qualities?"— having thus resolved with one mind, O King, the Haryaśvas set out along that path from which there is no turning back.
Having fixed his undivided mind upon the lotus feet of Hṛṣīkeśa— which shine forth within the *svarabrahman*— the sage wandered through the worlds;
yet, having heard from Nārada of the destruction of his virtuous sons, he was overcome with grief.

He lamented, grieving that his possession of excellent progeny had become a source of sorrows. Then Dakṣa, being consoled once more by the Unborn One (Brahmā), begot upon Pañcajanī thousands of sons, including the Valāśvas.
Commanded by their father to create progeny and firm in their vows,
they went to the Nārāyaṇa-lake where their own ancestors had attained perfection;
by merely touching its waters, the impurities of their hearts were completely shaken off.
Chanting the supreme Brahman, they performed great austerities there;
some subsisted on water for months, while others lived on air,
worshipping and repeatedly practicing this mantra dedicated to the Lord of Food (Iḍaspati).

"Oṃ, obeisances to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul, whose abode is pure goodness; we meditate upon Him, the Great Swan. O King of kings, having thus addressed them, the sage—whose mind was intent on the creation of progeny—[proceeded].
Approaching them, Nārada spoke these deceptive words as before:
"O daughters of Dakṣa, listen to my instruction as I speak;
O you who are devoted to your brothers, follow in the footsteps of your brothers."
"The brother who, knowing the dharma, follows the departure of his brothers—
that virtuous man, a kinsman of merit, rejoices together with the Maruts.
Having said this much, Nārada, whose vision is never in vain, departed.
O noble one, they too followed the path of their brothers; having gone together toward the west along the further bank of the river,
they have not yet returned, even as the final watches of the night draw on.
At that time, observing many portents, Prajāpati heard,
as before, of the destruction of his son caused by Nārada;
fainting from grief for his son, he became enraged at Nārada.
Having encountered the celestial sage, Śrī Dakṣa, his lower lip quivering with rage, spoke:
Śrī Dakṣa said:
"Alas! O wicked one, by you who bear the outward marks of a saint among us..."

An improper deed has been committed by children; the path of a mendicant has been shown to those who are not freed from the three debts and have not yet examined their karma. This obstacle to the highest good has brought sin upon both worlds.
"Thus, O Hare, you who are devoid of compassion and destroy the minds of the innocent,
wander shamelessly among the assembly of the Lord's attendants as a destroyer of His fame.
Are not the devotees of the Lord always intent upon showing grace to all living beings?"
Except for you— who are indeed a destroyer of friendship and a creator of enmity toward those who bear no enmity—
there could not be such detachment in men through you alone; yet you falsely consider this to be the severing of the bonds of affection and the attainment of peace.
A person does not know the sharpness of sense objects without experiencing them;
one becomes detached from them spontaneously, whereas those whose minds are distracted by others do not.
This is because you have [granted us] the state of householders who are virtuous and devoted to the performance of ritual duties.
"You have committed an intolerable offense against us, yet it was forgiven by you. O weaver, since you have again acted unkindly toward us,
therefore, O fool, there shall be no place for you to wander among the worlds."
Śrī Śuka said:
Nārada, who is esteemed by the virtuous, accepted that proposal with the words "So be it. For this is the mark of a saintly person: that the Lord himself endures all things.
Śrī Śuka said: Then the son of Pracetas, having been entreated by the Self-born Creator,
begot sixty daughters through Asiknī who were devoted to their father.
He gave ten daughters to Dharma, twelve to Indra, nine to Agni,
two each to Bhūta, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva, and others to Tārkṣya;
hear from me their names and those of their offspring.

By their offspring and descendants, the three worlds were filled. Listen now to the names of the wives of Dharma and their sons: Bhānu, Lambā, Kakud, Āmi, Viśvā, Sādhyā, Marutvatī, Vasu, Muhūrtā, and Saṅkalpā.
O King, from Bhanu was born Deva-ṛṣabha; from him came Indrasena.
From Lambā was born Vidyota, and from him came the Stanayitnavas.
From Kakud was born Saṅkaṭa, whose son was Kīkaṭa.
From Bhuva and Yāmī was born Svarga, from whom Nandi arose;
the Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā, and they are said to be childless; and from Sādhyā came the host of Sādhyas, whose son was Arthasiddhi.
Marutvān and Jayanta were born from Marutvatī;
Jayanta was a portion of Vāsudeva, whom the astrologers know as Upendra.
And from Muhūrtā were born the hosts of gods known as the Mauhūrtikas.

Indeed, those who bestow upon living beings the fruits produced by their respective times are known as Saṅkalpa; Kāma is the offspring of Saṅkalpa, born from Saṅkalpa. The Vasus are the eight sons of Vasu; hear their names from me.
Droṇa, Prāṇa, Dhruva, Arka, Agni, Doṣa, Vāstu, and Vibhāvasu;
from Droṇa’s beloved wife were born Harṣa, Śoka, Bhaya, and others;
Prāṇa’s wife was Urjasvatī, and their sons were Saha, Āyus, and Purojava.
Dharaṇī, the wife of Dhruva, gave birth to various cities.
Vāsanā, the wife of Arka, is recorded to have had sons such as Tarṣa and others.
Vasordhārā, the wife of Agni, had sons such as Draviṇaka and others.
Skanda was the son of the Kṛttikās; from him came Viśākha and the others.
Doṣa’s son was Śarvarīputra, who was a portion (kalā) of Hari in the form of Śiśumāra.
Vāstu was the son of Āṅgirasī, and his son was Viśvakarmā, the lord of forms.
From that [Agni] arose Manu Cākṣuṣa; the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas were the sons of Manu.
From Vibhāvasu (Fire) were born Uṣas, Vyuṣṭa, Rociṣ, and Ātapa.
Then there is Pañcayāma, by which living beings awaken for their activities.
Bhūtā gave birth to millions of Rudras who were like her in form. Raivata’s sons were Aja, Bhava, Bhīma, Vāma, Ugra, Vṛṣākapi,
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, and Mahat.
The other attendants of Rudra were fierce *pretas* and *vināyakas*.
Then Svadhā, the wife of Prajāpati Aṅgiras, [bore] the Pitṛs. Furthermore, Satī made the Atharvāṅgirasa Veda her son.
Kṛśāśva begot Dhūmaketu from his wife Arciṣmatī;
[and] from Dhiṣaṇā he begot Vedaśiras, Devala, Vayuna, and Manu.
Of Tārkṣya, Vinatā, Kadrū, Pataṅgī, and Yāminī were the wives.

Pataṅgī gave birth to the birds, and Yāminī to the locusts; Suparṇā gave birth to Garuḍa, the direct vehicle of the Lord of Sacrifice, as well as Anūru, the charioteer of the Sun; and Kadrū gave birth to numerous serpents.
O descendant of Bharata, the constellations beginning with Kṛttikā are the wives of the Moon;
however, due to the curse of Dakṣa, he remained childless by them, afflicted as he was by the seizure of consumption.
Having again propitiated him, Soma regained his digits that had been diminished during his waning.
Listen to the names of the mothers of the worlds, which bring them auspiciousness, as well as the names of the wives of Kaśyapa from whom this universe was born: Aditi,
Diti, Danu, Kāṣṭhā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, and Ilā.
From Krodhavāśā were born Muni, Tāmrā, Surabhi, Saramā, and Timi;
from Timi came the herds of aquatic creatures, and the beasts of prey were the offspring of Saramā.
O King, from Surabhi were born the buffaloes, the cows, and whatever other cloven-hoofed animals there are.
O King, from Tāmrā were born the hawks, vultures, and other birds; from the sage [Kardama] came the hosts of Apsarases; from Krodhavaśā were born the serpents, such as the Dandaśūkas;
and from Ilā were born all trees, as well as the Yātudhānas and Saurasas.
The Gandharvas were born from Ariṣṭā, and the cloven-hoofed and other animals from Kāṣṭhā.
There were sixty-one sons of Danu; hear now their principal ones:
Dvimūrdhā, Śambara, Ariṣṭa, Hayagrīva, and Vibhāvasu.
Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Svarbhānu, Kapila, Aruṇa, Puloman, Vṛṣaparvan, Ekacakra, Anutāpana,
Dhūmrakeśa, Virūpākṣa, Vipracitti, and Durjaya.
It is said that Namuci married Suprabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu; and the powerful Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, married Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Furthermore, [Yayāti] had four daughters of beautiful appearance who were the daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Upadānavī, Hayaśirā, Pulomā, and likewise Kālakā;
O King, Hiraṇyākṣa married Upadānavī, Kratu married Hayaśirā, and Ka married both Pulomā and Kālakā, the two daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Then the Blessed Kaśyapa, impelled by Brahmā, married them;
[so did] the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, those Dānavas skilled in battle.
Of those two, their father’s father had sixty thousand Yajñaghna-s.
O King, after he had gone to heaven, Vipracitti— who alone acted for the pleasure of Indra—
begot one hundred and one sons upon Siṃhikā;
Rāhu was the eldest, and the other hundred became known as the Ketus, having attained the status of planets.
Now, therefore, hear the lineage of Aditi in its proper sequence,
wherein the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa descended by means of his own portions:
Vivasvān, Aryamā, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, and Bhaga.

Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Varuṇa, Mitra, Śatru, and Urukrama—these were the names of Vivasvat’s sons. And from Vivasvat, the highly fortunate Saṃjñā bore the son Manu, known as Śrāddhadeva, as well as a twin pair: the god Yama and Yamī.
Having become a mare, she then gave birth to the two Nāsatyas on earth; Chāyā obtained Śanaiścara and Sāvarṇi Manu,
as well as a daughter, Tapatī, who chose Saṃvaraṇa as her husband.
Mātṛkā was the wife of Aryaman, and from them were born the Carṣaṇis as their sons;
it was there that the human race was indeed fashioned by Brahmā.
Pūṣan, who formerly ate ground flour, became childless and had his teeth broken.
He who laughed when Dakṣa became enraged, revealing his teeth,
had a daughter named Racanā, the wife of Tvaṣṭṛ and daughter of a Daitya;
from them were born Sanniveśa and the powerful Viśvarūpa.
The hosts of gods chose him as their nephew, even though he had been abandoned by his father Aṅgiras out of resentment. King Parīkṣit said: Śrī-Parīkṣit said:
"For what reason did the preceptor abandon the gods, who were his own?
O Blessed One, explain this impropriety of disciples toward their guru.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
O King, Indra— the path of the righteous having been transgressed by him due to the intoxication of sovereignty over the three worlds—
was surrounded by the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Ṛbhus,
Viśvedevas, Sādhyas, and the two Nāsatyas.
O descendant of Bharata, Maghavan was attended by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and sages who discourse on Brahman,
as well as by Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, birds, and serpents,
while being praised by them all.
Being sung to melodiously while seated upon his throne,
he was attended by a white parasol as beautiful as the orb of the moon,
and provided with other royal insignia of sovereignty, such as yak-tail fans and the like.
While he was resplendent together with his queen Paulomī, who shared half his throne,
he did not welcome the arrival of the Supreme Teacher of the gods and of himself with rising from his seat, offering a seat, or other marks of respect.
Even upon seeing Vācaspati, the best of sages and honored by gods and demons, arrive at the assembly, Indra did not rise from his seat. Then, the lordly sage Aṅgiras suddenly departed from there.

The wise one returned silently to his own home, indifferent to his great splendor. At that very moment, Indra, having awakened to his own offense against his guru, censured himself before the assembly by means of his own intellect.

"Alas! Indeed, something most unwholesome has been done by me, who am of feeble intellect, in that I, intoxicated by power, treated my guru with contempt in the assembly. What wise man would covet even the fortune of the Lord of the Three Worlds?"
"By that [ignorance] I have been led today to an asuric state, even though I am the lord of the gods.
Those who would say, 'No one should rise to greet him while he occupies the supreme position of Brahmā,' do not know the highest dharma."

Those who place their faith in the words of those teachers of evil paths, as they fall into the darkness below, surely sink like stone rafts. Then I approached the teacher of the immortals, a twice-born one of unfathomable intellect.
"I shall propitiate him by touching his feet with my head," thought Niśaṭha.
While Indra was reflecting thus, the Blessed One, through his internal power of illusion (*adhyātmamāyā*), caused Bṛhaspati to depart from Indra's house, leading him to an unseen destination.

Not having received instruction from his guru, the self-sovereign Lord, though examining [the matter] with His intellect and joined by the gods in meditation, found no peace for Himself. Upon hearing that, all the asuras took recourse to the counsel of Uśanas.
The arrogant assailants launched an attack against the gods;
their limbs, thighs, and arms pierced by the sharp arrows discharged by those [demons], they,
along with Indra, went for refuge to Brahmā with their necks bowed.
Seeing them thus afflicted, the Lord, the self-born and unborn Brahmā, spoke with supreme compassion, consoling them. Śrī Brahmā said:
"Alas! O best of gods, you have indeed committed a great misfortune.
Out of pride in your power, you did not honor that most excellent Brahmin, who was devoted to the Veda and self-controlled.
This defeat of yours at the hands of your enemies is the result of that very misconduct."
O gods, behold how those who were once prosperous have been ruined by their own enemies;
O Maghavan, look at these haters of the preceptor who were ruined for transgressing against him,
yet have now been restored to prosperity by devotedly propitiating Kāvya.

"Even the descendants of Bhṛgu, who are devoted to the gods, would take my very abode; for what do they care for heaven, they whose counsel is unbreakable and who have been instructed in the true meaning? No misfortunes befall those lords of men who hold the Brahmins, Govinda, and cows in high esteem."
"Quickly worship that omniform, ascetic son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the self-controlled brāhmaṇa;
if you will forgive his actions, he, being honored, will provide for your needs.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus addressed by Brahmā and freed from their distress,
they approached the sage, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, embraced him, and spoke as follows.
The gods said:

"We have arrived at your hermitage as guests; may it be well with you. O dear one, let the desire of our ancestors be fulfilled at this appropriate time, for the highest duty of virtuous sons is the service of their parents."
O Brahmin, this is true even for those with sons, let alone for celibate students (*brahmacārins*).
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the brother is the embodiment of Marutpati (Indra); and the mother is the very body of the Earth herself.
Compassion is the personified form of his sister, Dharma himself is the guest,
fire is the personified form of the approaching visitor, and all living beings are his own self.
Therefore, one should not cause distress or defeat to distressed ancestors.
"O dear one, by means of austerity, you ought to fulfill our request. We choose you, the most excellent knower of Brahman, as our preceptor and guru,
so that we may swiftly conquer our rivals through your splendor."
For they do not censure the salutation of the feet of the youngest brother in matters concerning wealth;
O Brahmin, except for the Vedic meters, age is not the cause of seniority.
The illustrious Ṛṣi said:
Requested by the hosts of gods to serve as their priest (*purohita*), that one of great austerity,
Viśvarūpa, being pleased, spoke to them in gentle words. Śrī Viśvarūpa said:

"O Lord, how could one like me, a disciple of yours, reject what is requested by the lords of the world— a deed censured by those of virtuous character and which squanders spiritual luster? That very act is said to be for one's own true benefit."

"For those who possess nothing, the wealth is indeed gleaned grain; by that alone have I performed the hospitable rites for the virtuous in this world. O lords, how could I perform a sacrificial office (*purodhāsa*) that is censurable, by which a wicked-minded man rejoices?
Nevertheless, how much more so should I not refuse what is requested by my gurus?"
"I shall accomplish everything requested by you, even at the cost of my life and wealth.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus given his promise to them, Viśvarūpa, the great ascetic, [proceeded].

Chosen for the office of priest, he performed his duties with supreme concentration; the all-pervading Lord, by means of the Vaiṣṇava lore, seized and took away from Mahendra the prosperity of the enemies of the gods, which was protected even by the science of Śukra.
The noble-minded Viśvarūpa spoke that [knowledge] to Mahendra, by which the powerful thousand-eyed one, being protected, conquered the army of the asuras. Śrī Rājā said:

"O Blessed One, tell me that armor consisting of Nārāyaṇa, protected by which the thousand-eyed Indra, as if in play, conquered the enemy soldiers along with their sacrificial offerings and enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds."
Just as [the gods], protected by him, conquered their murderous enemies in battle—
Śrī Bādarāyaṇa said:
The son of Tvaṣṭṛ, having been chosen as the family priest, spoke to Mahendra who questioned him.
"Nārada said: 'Listen now with a one-pointed mind to this armor known as Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī Viśvarūpa said:
'Having washed his feet and hands, sipped water for purification (ācamana), and holding the sacred grass (pavitra) in his hand, he should face the north.'"
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras upon his own limbs and hands, restrained in speech and pure,
he should don the supreme armor of Nārāyaṇa when fear approaches—
placing it on the feet, the knees, the thighs, the belly, the heart, and the chest.
One should place the syllables beginning with *oṃ* on the mouth and the head in successive order; or alternatively, one may do so in reverse order, starting with "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hands using the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should assign the syllables beginning with *pra* and ending with *ya* to the joints of the fingers and the thumb;
one should place the syllable *oṃ* at the heart, the syllable *vi* on the head,
the syllable *ṣa* between the eyebrows, and the syllable *ṇa* with the topknot (*śikhā*).
One should apply the letter *ve* to the two eyes and the letter *na* to all the joints;
then, aiming at the weapon with the letter *ma*, the wise one should become the embodiment of the mantra.
One should direct that [mantra], ending in *phaṭ* and accompanied by the *visarga*, toward all directions.
Saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," one should meditate upon the supreme Self as the object of meditation, endowed with the six potencies;
one should recite this mantra, which is the embodiment of knowledge, splendor, and austerity.

Om! May Hari, who has placed his lotus feet upon the back of the king of birds and who possesses eight arms endowed with eight divine qualities, grant me complete protection—he who holds a shield, sword, mace, arrows, bow, and noose against formidable enemies.
In the waters, may he in the form of the Fish protect me from the hosts of aquatic creatures and from the noose of Varuṇa.
May Vāmana, the deceptive ascetic, protect me on dry land; may Trivikrama protect me in the sky;

and in difficult places such as forests and the front lines of battle, may the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of the leaders of the demon hosts, protect me—he at whose release of a great, boisterous laugh the quarters of the earth resounded and the fetuses fell from their wombs.
May that Boar, who upheld the earth with his tusk and was like a sacrifice on the path, protect me;

may Rāma, the elder brother of Bharata, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, protect us while dwelling among the mountain peaks. May Nārāyaṇa protect me from all transgressions of fierce dharma, and may Nara protect me from negligence.

May Kapila, the Lord of Yoga and Master of the qualities, who was given by You through the power of yoga, protect me from the bondage of karma. May Sanatkumāra protect me from the god of desire; may Hayagrīva protect me on the path from the offense against the gods. May Kūrma, the best of divine sages, protect me from the failure to worship the Supreme Person; and may Hari protect me from every hell.
May the blessed Dhanvantari protect me from unwholesome food; may Ṛṣabha, who has conquered his self, protect me from the fear of dualities;
may Yajña descend from the world of Janaloka; may Bala [protect] from the Gaṇas; and may the Lord of Serpents [protect] from Krodhavaśa.
May the blessed Dvaipāyana protect me from lack of awakening; and may Buddha protect me from the negligence of the multitude of heretics.
May Kalki, who has taken a vast incarnation for the protection of Dharma, protect me from the impurity of time in the Kali age.

May Keśava protect me with his mace in the morning; may Govinda, holding his flute, protect me at dawn; may Nārāyaṇa, whose power is exalted, protect me in the forenoon; and may Viṣṇu, whose hand holds the lord of serpents, protect me at midday.
May the god Madhudhrogradhanvā protect me in the afternoon; may Mādhava protect me in the evening. May Hṛṣīkeśa protect me at dusk, and may Padmanābha alone protect me at midnight.
May the Lord Śrīvatsadhāmā protect me in the latter part of the night, and may the Lord Janārdana, bearing a sword, protect me at dawn.
May Dāmodara protect us at every junction of time; may the Lord Viśveśvara, the embodiment of Time, protect us at dawn.

May the discus, set in motion by the Blessed One, with its rim blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, revolving on all sides—burn, burn quickly the enemy host, just as the wind-fanned fire consumes dry grass.

O mace, with sparks like the touch of a thunderbolt, crush, crush him! O beloved of the Unconquered One, grind to powder the Kuṣmāṇḍas, Vaināyakas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Grahas; crush the enemies!
You who possess the terrible gaze of Yātudhānas, Pramathas, Pretas, Mātṛs, Piśācas, and the seizing spirits of Brahmins!
O Lord of the Thunderbolt, filled by Kṛṣṇa, scatter the enemy with your terrifying roar, making their hearts tremble.

Directed by the Lord, cut, cut through the enemy host with your excellent sword of sharp edge! O you whose shield bears the moon, cover their eyes; seize the sight of my enemies, those of sinful vision!
O Blessed One, whatever fear we have had from the planets, from comets, and from men;
from reptiles, from fanged beasts, from malevolent spirits, and from calamities—
all these [are dispelled] by the chanting of Your names and forms.
May those who are obstacles to our welfare perish instantly.
May the Lord Garuḍa— the master consisting of the Vedas, whose praise is the *stobha*—
and Viṣvaksena protect us from all misfortunes by means of their own names.
May the name, form, vehicles, and weapons of Hari— along with His attendants and ornaments— protect us from all calamities, as well as our intellect, senses, mind, and vital breaths;
for in reality, the Blessed Lord alone is both that which exists and that which does not exist.
"By this truth, may all our afflictions come to an end.
Just as He Himself, though free from conceptual differentiation, assumes through His own *māyā* the powers known as ornaments, weapons, and emblems, by virtue of the experience of His oneness."
By that very measure of truth, may the omniscient Lord Hari,
who is omnipresent, protect us always and everywhere with all His own forms.
May the Lord Nṛsiṃha be present in the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, above, below, on all sides, within, and without.

"O Maghavan, by your own roar, you shall cause all worldly fear to vanish, having swallowed up all other splendors with your own brilliance. This armor, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, has been declared; clad in it, you will swiftly conquer the leaders of the hosts of asuras."
Whoever wears this [mantra] is immediately liberated from whatever fear he sees with his eyes or touches with his feet;
for one who maintains this knowledge, there shall be no fear from any quarter.
From kings, thieves, predatory beasts, and the like, as well as from diseases and other afflictions, this knowledge has never failed him.
Long ago, a certain twice-born man named Kauśika, possessing this science,
abandoned his own body through the practice of yoga in a desert region.
Once, Citraratha, the lord of the Gandharvas, surrounded by women, was traveling in his celestial chariot over that place where the dwellings of the twice-born were located; suddenly,
he and his chariot fell from the sky, headlong.
At the word of the Vālakhilyas, he was filled with wonder; taking the bones, he cast them into the Prācī-sarasvatī, bathed there, and returned to his own abode.
Śrī Śuka said:
All beings bow down to one who hears this at the proper time and who maintains it with reverence; such a person is liberated from all fear.
Having acquired this knowledge from Viśvarūpa, Indra [became] the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Having utterly defeated the asuras in battle, he enjoyed the fortune of the three worlds.
Śrī Śuka said:
O descendant of Bharata, Viśvarūpa had three heads.
O King, we have heard that he was known as Somapītha, Surāpītha, and Annāda;
for on the sacrificial grass (barhis), he openly and with great reverence offered a portion to the gods,
whose ancestors were the gods themselves.
For he himself had assigned a share for the asuras while remaining invisible;
yet, driven by the influence of maternal affection, he offered that share to the sacrificer.
The Lord of the Gods [perceived] that offense against the gods and his deception regarding dharma.

Seeing this, he was terrified and in his wrath swiftly severed their heads. That head of his which had been accustomed to drinking Soma became a *kapiñjala* partridge; that which drank wine became a *kalaviṅka*; and that which ate food became a *tittiri*.
Although he was the Lord, Hari took the sin of Brahman-slaughter upon himself with his cupped hands;
at the end of a year, for the purification of all beings, he distributed that evil fourfold among the earth, water, trees, and women.
The earth accepted a fourth part by means of the boon of filling up its excavations;
thus, the form of the Brahman-slaying appears on the ground as barren soil.
By the boon of regrowth after being cut, the trees accepted a fourth part.
The sin of killing a brāhmaṇa appeared among them in the form of their exudation;
by means of a boon for eternal desire, women took a fourth part of that sin,
and that sin appears in them month after month in the form of menstrual flow.
By means of a boon consisting of an abundance of material substance, the waters took upon themselves a fourth part of the impurity.
Seeing that [impurity] in the form of bubbles and foam within them, he [the Lord] removed it by casting it away.
Thereupon, Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, offered an oblation to Indra as his enemy.
"O enemy of Indra, grow strong; do not delay; slay the enemy!
Then, from the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, there arose one of terrible appearance, like the God of Death at the end of an eon for all the worlds.
Increasing on all sides day by day to the size of an arrow,
resembling a scorched mountain, with the luster of a mass of evening clouds,

Having impaled the two worlds (Heaven and Earth) upon his blazing trident,
he was dancing and roaring, shaking the earth with his foot,
and drinking in the vault of the sky with his cavern-deep mouth.
Seeing him licking the three worlds with his tongue as he repeatedly yawned with his massive, fierce fangs,
all the inhabitants of the world were terrified and fled in the ten directions.
He by whom these worlds were enveloped through his ascetic power in the form of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son—
he indeed was called Vṛtra, the sinful and most terrible one;
the preeminent gods, accompanied by their hosts, rushed upon him and slew him.
With floods of their own respective divine missiles and weapons, he swallowed them all entirely.
Then they were all struck with wonder and despondent, their splendor eclipsed; with concentrated minds, they approached the Original Person who was facing toward them.
The gods said:

"O wind, ether, fire, water, and earth—the three worlds, Brahmā and the others, and we ourselves who tremble before him—to whom we offer tribute, even Death himself fears; therefore, he is our refuge."
A fool indeed approaches one who is free from pride, whose desires are fulfilled, who is content with his own gains, and who is perfectly tranquil,
just as one tries to cross the ocean with the claw of a dog. For it was by binding the world to the great horn of that [Lord] like a boat, that Manu crossed over the impassable [ocean].
He alone is surely our protector from the insurmountable fear of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, even though he is but a water-dweller;

for in the past, when the self-born Brahmā had fallen alone from his lotus seat into the waters of dissolution—terrible with the roar of surging winds and waves—he crossed over that very danger by means of Him. May He be our final refuge.
He who alone is the Lord who, by His own *māyā*, created us, and through whom we create the universe;
yet we, who imagine ourselves to be separate lords, do not perceive His manifest form even as He exerts Himself before us.
He who, though eternally present among gods, sages, animals, and men, [protects] us when we are being severely oppressed by our enemies.

Having manifested incarnations through his own *māyā* by means of various forms, he makes them his own and protects them age after age. To that very God, our own deity, the supreme, the primordial, the universal Puruṣa who is distinct [from all else], we all go for refuge—he who is worthy of being sought for shelter; may that Great-Souled One bestow peace upon us.
Śrī Śuka said:
O great king, while the gods were thus standing before him,
the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace appeared in the western direction.

Seeing him on the ground— his eyes like blossoming autumn lotuses, attended by sixteen companions equal to himself, and adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem— all were overwhelmed by the joy of his gaze.
O King, falling prostrate like a staff, they rose slowly and offered praise.
The glorious gods said:
"Salutations to You, whose potency is sacrifice; salutations also to You, the Supreme Age."
Salutations to You who possess the discus as Your weapon; salutations to You who are well-invoked by many.
For that supreme abode of Yours, the Lord of the three paths of existence, no one within the scope of the created world is capable of knowing, O Creator.

Oṃ, obeisances unto You, O Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Original Person, Great Person, O Being of Great Majesty! O Supreme Auspiciousness, Supreme Well-being, Supreme Compassionate One, Sole Support of the Universe, Sole Lord of the World, Sovereign of All, Lord of Lakṣmī!

[Salutations] by those wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsas*, whose dharma of the highest *parivrājaka* state has been made perfectly clear and whose door of darkness has been flung open through the supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the self.
O Lord, since the world of the self has been unveiled within your mind, you have personally experienced the realization of your own innate bliss;

yet this mode of your sporting appears difficult to comprehend, in that— being without refuge, bodiless, and indifferent to our collective existence— you, though yourself changeless and devoid of qualities, create,
protect, and withdraw this world which possesses qualities.

Now, we truly do not know whether Your Honor here, like Devadatta, has fallen into the discharge of the modes and, being subject to another, experiences the fruit of your own good and evil deeds; or whether, delighting in the Self, peaceful in nature, and possessing correct vision, you remain indifferent.

Indeed, there is no contradiction regarding these two aspects in the Blessed Lord, who possesses an immeasurable multitude of qualities, whose majesty is unfathomable, and in whom all dispute has no place for those who rely on internal organs clouded by modern conceptualizations, conjectures, deliberations, fallacious proofs, and fallacious logic, as well as by the teachings of various schools.
For in Him, who is entirely free from all that consists of *māyā*, what indeed could be impossible when He alone, having withdrawn His own *māyā*, remains?
He appears as if possessing two forms, yet there is no duality of nature because He lacks a second essence (BhP 06.09.037).
You follow the minds of those with even or uneven intellects, just as a segment of rope follows the perceptions of [those who mistake it for] a snake and so forth (BhP 06.09.038).

For He alone is the true nature of all things, the Lord of All, the cause of the causes of the entire universe; and because He is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of all, He is characterized by the manifestation of all qualities.
Only one remained.

Then indeed, those supreme devotees— by whom even a single drop from the ocean of the nectar of Your majesty, once tasted, causes a continuous bliss to overflow within their own minds, thereby causing them to forget the mere semblance of the fragments of pleasure found in the objects of sight and hearing— [remained].

O Slayer of Madhu, how indeed could these saintly ones—who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One, the beloved friend and Self of all beings—whose minds are utterly and continuously at peace, ever abandon the service of Your lotus feet? For they are experts in their own true interest and cherish their own welfare; yet, where is there a cessation of this cycle of worldly existence other than in that service?
O Soul of the three worlds, O Abode, O Trivikrama, O Three-eyed One, O You whose majesty is enchanting to the three worlds!

Even the sons of Diti and Danu are Your own manifestations; yet, thinking "this is the time for their subjugation," O Wielder of the Staff, You have by Your own Māyā assumed the forms of gods, humans, beasts, and mixed aquatic creatures, and have inflicted punishment upon them according to their offenses—just so, [punish] this one as well.
O Blessed One, slay the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, if you so intend;

for us— your own followers who are prostrate before you, O Hari, whose hearts are bound by the fetters of meditation upon Your pair of lotus feet, and who have been made Your own by the disclosure of Your true nature— there is [this grace] through the glance of Your clear, beautiful, and cool smile, colored with compassion, and through the digit of the nectar of the sweet juice of Your mouth.
O sinless one, you ought to pacify our inner torment.
Now, O Blessed One, for you whose divine play consists of the illusory power (*māyā*) that serves as the cause for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire world—
[you who exist] within the hearts of all living beings and externally as well, in the form of Brahman, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and in the form of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

And for that Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, whose body is space, who is the witness of all cognitions, and who experiences the specific distinctions of place, time, and bodily state through the perception of their respective substrates— how much of its particular nature could possibly be made known here,
any more than the nature of fire can be conveyed by means of sparks and the like?

Therefore, please yourself provide for us the shade of the hundred-petaled lotus of the feet of Your Lordship, our supreme guru— the shade that pacifies the exhaustion of this manifold, wretched cycle of worldly existence— for we have approached You with whatever desire brought us here.
Furthermore, O Lord, slay the son of Tvaṣṭṛ who is devouring the three worlds.
O Kṛṣṇa, by whom our splendors, missiles, and weapons have been swallowed—

salutations to You, the Swan, whose abode is the heart-lake, the Witness, the Dark One of purified fame, who is beyond all effort, the gatherer of the virtuous, and who, at the end of the journey for travelers through worldly existence, grants the sought-after goal; salutations to You, Hari.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus praised with devotion by the gods, Hari,
hearing their hymn of praise, spoke to them with approval.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am pleased with you, O best of gods, because of this knowledge of my worship,
by which men attain the memory of their own sovereignty and devotion unto me."
O best of the wise, when I am pleased, what is difficult to attain? Nevertheless, one whose mind is fixed on me alone as the sole goal, knowing the truth, desires nothing other than Me.
The wretched man, who perceives only material objects as real, does not know his own true welfare.
If he, being of such a nature himself, should withhold those [teachings] even while the other desires them—
though he knows the supreme good— he does not speak it to one who is ignorant, for action [must be appropriate]. Indeed,
the best of physicians does not give unwholesome food even to a sick man who craves it.
"O Maghavan, go; may it be well with you. Ask Dadhyañc, the best of sages, whose essence is knowledge, vows, and austerity, for his body without delay.
He, Dadhyañc, then imparted the undivided Brahman to the Aśvins.
Or rather, it was the one named Aśvaśiras who granted immortality to those two;
for Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa gave Tvaṣṭṛ an invulnerable armor consisting of my essence,
which Tvaṣṭṛ then gave to Viśvarūpa, and you subsequently destroyed that.
Requested by you both, the Ashvins, that knower of dharma will give his limbs; then,
with those [limbs], he— strengthened by my splendor— will fashion with the help of Vishvakarman the most excellent of weapons, by which he shall sever the head of Vritra.
"When he has been slain, you shall regain your splendor, weapons, missiles, and wealth; may prosperity be yours, for they shall no longer harm those who are devoted to Me.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:

Having thus instructed Indra, the Blessed Lord Hari, the creator of the universe, vanished right there while the gods were looking on with unblinking eyes. Likewise, the great seer of the Atharva Veda was entreated by the gods.
Rejoicing, O descendant of Bharata, he spoke this as if laughing:
