"O you gods, do you not know that at the time of death,
there is for embodied beings an unbearable hostility that robs them of their consciousness?"
For living beings who desire to live, the self is the most beloved object desired here in this world.
Who would venture to give that away to Viṣṇu when he comes as a beggar?
The goddesses said:
O Brahmin, what indeed is so difficult for great souls like you to renounce— those who are compassionate toward all beings and whose deeds are honored by those of virtuous fame?
Surely, people intent on their own self-interest do not understand the distress of others.
"If he knows it, he would not ask; if he is the Lord, he would not say 'no'.
The venerable sage said:
"I have addressed you because I desire to hear from you about dharma."
O lords, I now abandon this very Self who is dear to you, I who am a man that, through this transient body, seeks neither virtue nor fame,
but only out of compassion for living beings— such a person is to be pitied even by the immobile plants.
This is the extent of the imperishable dharma practiced by those of virtuous renown:
that one’s own self grieves at the grief of living beings and rejoices at their joy.
Alas, what wretchedness! What misery! To be attached to things belonging to others, which are as fleeting as a moment!
"That which a mortal cannot benefit with his own interests or through conflicts with his own kinsmen...
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
"Having thus resolved, Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa [prepared] his body..."
Directing his self toward the Supreme Lord, the Brahman, he abandoned [his body];
with his senses, life-breath, mind, and intellect restrained, perceiving reality and having his bonds destroyed,
he remained established in supreme yoga and did not perceive that his body had departed.
Then Indra, uplifted by the powers of the sage and endowed with the splendor of the Blessed One, raised the thunderbolt fashioned by Viśvakarman;
surrounded by all the hosts of gods, he shone atop the lordly elephant.
Being praised by hosts of sages as if gladdening the three worlds, O King,
he rushed toward his enemy Vṛtra, who was surrounded by the leaders of the Asura armies,
with such power that he resembled the enraged Rudra attacking Antaka.
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā age, in the first yuga, a most terrible battle took place between the gods and the asuras on the banks of the Narmadā.
[The gods were] accompanied by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, the two Aśvins, the Pitṛs, and the Fires.
O King, seeing Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, wielding the thunderbolt and resplendent with his own glory, accompanied by the Maruts, Ṛbhus, Sādhyas, and Viśvedevas,
the demons led by Vṛtra could not endure him in battle.
Namuci, Śambara, Anarvā, Dvimūrdhan, the asura Ṛṣabha,
Hayagrīva, Śaṅkuśiras, Vipracitti, Ayomukha,
Puloman, Vṛṣaparvan, Praheti, Heti, and Utkala.
Thousands of Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
led by Sumālin and Māli and adorned with golden ornaments,
blocked the vanguard of Indra’s army, which was difficult even for Death to approach.
Undaunted and intoxicated with pride, they assailed him with lion-like roars,
using maces, iron clubs, arrows, spears,
mallets, and lances; with pikes, battle-axes, swords, *śataghnīs*, and *bhuśuṇḍis*.
They showered weapons and missiles from all sides upon the bulls among the gods;
yet they were not seen, being completely covered on every side by nets of arrows,
like stars obscured by thick clouds in the sky as they fall one after another in continuous succession.
Those showers of weapons and missiles did not reach the celestial soldiers;
severed by the gods with their swift hands in mid-air, they were split into a thousand pieces.
Then, their floods of weapons and missiles being exhausted, [the demons attacked] with mountain peaks, trees, and stones.
They rained down upon the army of the gods and cut them down as before;
then, seeing those [demons] unhurt and safe despite the multitude of weapons and missiles,
the lords of Vṛtra’s hosts terrified the soldiers of Indra with trees, stones, and various mountain peaks.
All the efforts made by the Daityas against the hosts of gods became fruitless,

just as harsh words uttered by the lowly toward great men who are well-disposed toward Kṛṣṇa; seeing their own exertions rendered vain, those who were undevoted to Hari had the pride of battle destroyed.
Having abandoned their leader at the front of the battle, they set their minds on flight, having surrendered their strength.
Seeing those followers fleeing, the wise Vṛtra spoke these words,
laughing as he beheld the army broken by intense fear and in retreat.
The hero among men spoke these timely and pleasing words to the wise ones:
"O Vipracitti, Namuci, Puloman, Maya, Anarvan, and Śambara, listen to me!
For one who is born, death is certain from every side, and no remedy for it has been devised here."
If from this [practice] one gains the world and fame, who indeed would not choose such death?

Two types of death are highly esteemed here as difficult to attain: that which occurs when one devoted to yoga abandons the body after conquering the life-force through the concentration on Brahman; and that which occurs when a leader, never turning back, falls upon the hero’s bed.
Śrī Śuka said: O King, though their husband thus spoke words of dharma, they, being bewildered and intent on flight, did not heed his speech at all.
Seeing his Asura army being shattered and driven away like one who is helpless by the gods acting in accordance with Time, the bull among Asuras,
Indra’s enemy, became enraged and filled with indignation.
O King, having warded them off with his might and rebuked them, he spoke these words:
"What is the use of killing those who flee after being struck from behind by their mother’s cries?
For the slaughter of the terrified is neither praiseworthy nor leads to heaven for those who pride themselves on their heroism."
"If you have faith in this battle, or if there is even a slight essence [of purpose] in your hearts, O petty ones,
stand before me for a moment— if you have no longing for vulgar pleasures.
Thus, the enraged one, terrifying his enemies with his form, addressed the hosts of gods.
He, possessing immense vital power, let out a roar by which all the worlds were deprived of their senses;
by that very sound of Vṛtra’s bursting forth, all the hosts of gods fell to the ground in a swoon, as if struck by a thunderbolt.

Intoxicated by the pride of battle, he crushed the distressed army of the gods with his feet; with eyes closed in pain, they were trampled as he brandished his spear with such vigor that he made the earth tremble, like a rutting leader of an elephant herd crushing a forest.
Seeing him, the wielder of the thunderbolt, filled with extreme indignation, rushed at his enemy with a great mace.

As it came flying toward him, that Suduḥsahā was thrown back; he, the enemy of Indra, seized it with his left hand as if in play. Greatly enraged by her, O King, that one of immense prowess struck the elephant of Mahendra on the frontal globes with his mace while roaring in battle; all honored that deed.
Airāvata, struck by Vṛtra’s mace, reeled like a mountain hit by a thunderbolt;
with his mouth gashed, Indra fled along with him, vomiting blood and deeply afflicted, though he still bore his seven bows.
The high-souled [Vṛtra] did not hurl his mace again at him, whose horses were collapsed and whose mind was despondent.
Indra stood there, his horses free from pain and injury due to the touch of the hand that flowed with nectar.
Seeing that enemy— the wielder of the thunderbolt who had slain his brother—
and remembering that cruel, sinful deed, he spoke while laughing out of grief and delusion.
Śrī Vṛtra said:
"By good fortune, you have appeared before me as my enemy—you who are a killer of a brāhmaṇa, a killer of your guru, and a killer of your brother.
By good fortune, O most wretched one, I shall today be freed from my debt to you, whose heart is like a stone, soon pierced by my trident."

He who, desiring heaven, mercilessly severed with a sword the heads of our elder— a twice-born knower of the Self, sinless and initiated— after placing his trust in him, like the head of a sacrificial animal; you, who have been abandoned by fortune, modesty, compassion, and fame, and are censured by man-eaters for your own deed.
The vultures devour my body with difficulty as it is pierced by my own trident, even though I have not touched fire;
and those others here who, being ignorant and cruel, strike me with raised weapons—
I worship them along with the lords of beings and their hosts through my throat, which has been pierced by the sharpened trident.
Moreover, O Hero, if Hari here should indeed strike off my head with his thunderbolt after crushing me,
I shall then become free from debt by offering myself as a sacrifice to all beings and take refuge at the feet of the wise.
O Lord of the Gods, why do you not hurl your infallible thunderbolt at me, your enemy, who stands right before you?
"Do not have any doubt; let it not be as fruitless as a thunderbolt failing its mark or a supplication made to a miser.
Indeed, O Śakra, this thunderbolt has been sharpened by your own splendor and by the ascetic power of Dadhīci, who was empowered by Hari.
With that very weapon, slay the enemy, for Viṣṇu directs you; where there is Hari, there is victory, prosperity, and all virtues."

Having fixed my mind, as Saṅkarṣaṇa instructed us, upon Your lotus feet, I shall—shaken from the worldly snares by the thunderbolt-like force of Your power and having cast aside all worldly concerns—attain the state of a sage.
Indeed, whatever riches belong to Your own people who possess single-minded devotion, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld; [all those I seek].
O Śakra, that which consists of lack of generosity, hatred, agitation, mental distress, intoxication, strife, calamity,
and excessive exertion— our Lord ordains these for a man as the destruction of the efforts toward the three goals of life (traivargika).
Therefore, one may infer the grace of the Blessed One, which is difficult to obtain and accessible only to those who possess nothing else.
O Hari, may I once again become the servant of servants at the sole root of Your feet; may my mind remember Your qualities, my speech sing them, and my body perform service for You.
Neither the vault of heaven, nor the status of Brahmā, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the waters is desired by me.
O most excellent one, I do not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth if they exclude you;

O lotus-eyed one, my mind, distressed and longing for its beloved who has departed, yearns to see you, just as fledglings with undeveloped wings long for their mother, as thirsty calves long for milk, or as a sorrowful wife longs for her absent husband.

"O Lord, as I wander through the cycle of worldly existence by my own karma, may I never again have friendship with those who belong to the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), while my mind remains attached to self, children, wife, and home through Your illusory power (māyā).
The venerable sage said:
O King, thus desiring to cast off his body in battle and considering death preferable to victory,
he seized a spear and rushed at the Lord of the Gods, just as Kaiṭabha once assailed the Great Person within the waters.
Then the lord of the Asuras, brandishing his spear with speed— its tip as fierce as the fire at the end of an eon— [attacked].
Having hurled it at Mahendra and roared, the hero said in rage, "You are slain, O sinner!
Seeing that weapon falling through the sky— difficult to behold like a trembling meteor or a falling planet—
the wielder of the thunderbolt, undaunted, severed with his hundred-jointed *vajra* both that weapon and the arm of the enemy which resembled the coil of the king of serpents.
With one arm severed by the *parigha* (iron club), Vṛtra, filled with rage, approached Indra who held the thunderbolt and struck him on the jaw;
then the thunderbolt fell from Maghavan’s hand, as did the celestial elephant. The hosts of gods, asuras, cāraṇas, and siddhas marveled at that most wonderful deed of Vṛtra.
Seeing that great danger from Indra, they failed to worship him and cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas!
Indra, filled with shame, could not take back the thunderbolt that had fallen from his hand in the presence of the enemy.
Vṛtra said to him, "O Hara, take up the thunderbolt and slay your own enemy; this is no time for despondency."
Among those who desire to fight and who are aggressors, victory never belongs permanently to one side;
this is true for all except for the Supreme Self— the omniscient, primordial, eternal Person, the Lord of creation, dissolution,
and maintenance, under whose control these worlds and their guardians breathe helplessly.
Like birds bound by a net, they are held fast; that Time alone is the cause here in this world.
Vitality, fortitude, strength, life-breath, immortality, and even death—all these are Time.
Failing to understand Him as the cause, the dull-witted person considers himself to be the cause.
"Just as a woman made of wood, or as a deer made of leaves, so too,
O Maghavan, know that all beings are dependent upon the Lord.
Puruṣa, Prakṛti, the manifest, the self, the elements, the senses, and the subconscious impressions [are all under His control]."
At the beginning of creation, they are unable to act without His grace;
thus, the ignorant man considers himself the Lord when he is not the Lord,
thinking that he creates beings by means of the elements and devours those beings through them himself.
For at that time, whatever blessings a person may desire— longevity, prosperity, fame, sovereignty, and so forth— occur even without their seeking them, yet their opposites likewise occur.
Therefore, whether there be infamy or glory, victory or defeat, it is the same.
One should be equanimous toward pleasure and pain, as well as toward death and life.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*, not of the self (*ātman*);
he who knows the self to be the witness therein is not bound.
Behold me, O enemy, conquered in battle with my weapons and arms severed, though I was striving to the best of my power with the desire to take your life;
for this battle is a wager of lives, with arrows as dice and mounts as the stakes.
"In this matter, it is not known who will be victorious and who will be defeated.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard Vṛtra's words, which were free from falsehood, Indra honored them.
Having seized his thunderbolt and overcome with amazement, he laughed and said to him.
Indra said:
"O Dānava, you have achieved perfection, for your intellect is such as this!"

O Lord, by being devoted with your whole being to the Self, the Friend, and the Sovereign of the World, you have indeed crossed over the illusory power of Viṣṇu that deludes all people; for, having abandoned the demonic disposition, you have attained the state of a Great Being.

This is indeed a great wonder: that your mind is firmly fixed upon Vāsudeva, the Blessed Lord, who is the self of pure goodness (*sattva*), even though you are of a nature characterized by passion (*rajas*).
For one whose devotion is directed toward the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign of ultimate liberation—
"What need have those who sport in the ocean of nectar for the water collected in small pits?
Śrī Śuka said:
"O King, thus did they speak to one another out of a desire to know the dharma."

The two of great prowess, Indra and Vṛtra, the lords of battle, fought each other. O noble one, having whirled a terrible iron club in his left hand, Vṛtra, the subduer of enemies, hurled it at Indra.
The Lord, with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, simultaneously severed Vṛtra’s club-like arm and his trunk, which resembled an elephant’s trunk;
with both arms lopped off at the roots, the asura shone, streaming with blood.
Like a wingless Garuḍa struck by the wielder of the thunderbolt and fallen from the sky,
or like a great serpent of immense breath and prowess attacking an elephant,
the Daitya lay upon the ground with his lower jaw on the earth and his upper jaw raised toward the heavens.
With a mouth as deep as the sky and a terrifying tongue flickering out,
with fangs like the god of death, he seemed to swallow the three worlds;
possessing an exceedingly massive body, he violently hurled mountains aside.
Like a mountain king walking on foot, grinding the earth with his feet,
he approached and seized the wielder of the thunderbolt along with his mount.
Seeing him swallowed by Vṛtra, the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, [were struck with fear].
"Alas, what misery! cried the sages along with the great seers in despair.
"Though he has been swallowed by the lord of the Asuras, the Great Person, equipped as he is with his armor and the power of his *yogamāyā*, has not entered his belly."
Having split open her womb with his thunderbolt, the powerful Lord, the slayer of Bala,
emerged and severed the head of the enemy with his might, as if it were a mountain peak. But the thunderbolt, moving with great speed and whirling all around, cut through her neck.
He struck him down in as many days as there were in the Vārtrahatya sacrifice of the Jyotiṣṭoma cycle.
Then, the kettledrums resounded in the sky, and the Gandharvas, Siddhas, along with hosts of sages,
praised him with mantras containing the name of the slayer of Vṛtra and joyfully showered him with flowers.
O subduer of enemies, as all the gods looked on, the light of the self that had emerged from Vṛtra’s body attained the world of the unconditioned (aloka).
Śrī Śuka said:
O Giver of Abundance, when Vṛtra was slain, the three worlds— along with their guardians— immediately became free from feverish distress, their senses at peace, even though they were bereft of Śakra.
So too did the gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, Daityas, and the followers of the gods themselves.
Then Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the others returned to their respective abodes.
King Parīkṣit said:
"O sage, I wish to hear the cause of Indra's lack of peace."
Since the gods were made happy by him, how could there be any suffering for Hari?
Śrī Śuka said:
All the gods, together with the sages, were greatly agitated by the prowess of Vṛtra.
Seeking to kill him, he entreated Indra; but Indra, fearing the great slaughter, did not wish to do so.
Indra said:
"O tree, having become a woman, wash away with water the sin arising from the killing of Viśvarūpa."
"Where shall I wipe away the sin of slaying Vṛtra, while you all look on with favor?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard that, the sages spoke thus to Mahendra.

"We shall perform the horse sacrifice for you; may prosperity be yours, do not fear. "By sacrificing to the Supreme Person, the Lord, the Divine Nārāyaṇa, through the horse sacrifice, you shall be liberated even from the slaughter of the world."
Even a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a father, a killer of a cow, a killer of a mother, or a killer of a teacher—
even a dog-eater or a Pulkasa— would be purified by the chanting of His name. He is [purified] by the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) performed by us with faith.
"Even by slaying all that is moving and unmoving along with its inhabitants, you are not tainted; what need is there to mention the subduing of a wicked one?
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus urged by the brahmins, Indra slew his enemy.

When he was slain, the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa fell upon Vṛṣākapi; because of that, Indra suffered great distress, yet peace entered him. Indeed, even virtues do not bring happiness to one who is ashamed and has become subject to public reproach.
He saw her running after him, appearing like a Cāṇḍāla woman;
her limbs were trembling with old age, she was seized by consumption, and she wore a garment of blood.
With her gray hair disheveled, she cried out, "Stop! Stop!"
O lord of the people, O king, the thousand-eyed Indra, having gone to the sky and perceived her polluting the path with the sweet fragrance of her fish-like scent,
quickly entered the north-eastern direction, the Mānasa lake.
There, the messenger of Agni, deprived of his enjoyment, dwelt for a thousand years within the fibers of a lotus stalk, unobserved,
contemplating how he might be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
meanwhile, Nahuṣa, by the power and majesty of his knowledge, austerity, and yoga, ruled over the celestial realm of Triṇāka.
His intellect blinded by the intoxication of wealth and power, he was led to the state of animals by the wife of Indra.

Then, summoned by the words of Brahmā, his sins were warded off by meditation that bears truth; yet the evil one, his vigor destroyed by the goddess of the quarters, could not overcome him who was protected by the wife of Viṣṇu.
O descendant of Bharata, the celestial sages approached him and duly initiated him with the horse sacrifice, which is indeed the worship of the Supreme Person. Then,
while the Supreme Person, the self who embodies all the gods, was being worshipped, [the sacrifice proceeded].

O King, although the accumulation of sin resulting from the slaughter of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son was immense, it was rendered void by that very horse-sacrifice performed by Mahendra with the assistance of the exponents of the Vedas,
just as mist is dispelled by the sun.

Having performed the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*) as prescribed, with the ancient Lord of Sacrifice (*adhiyajña-puruṣa*) present along with Marīci and the other sages, Indra became great, his sins shaken off.
This great narrative is a washing away of all sins and a glorification of Him whose feet are the sacred ford (*tīrthapada*).

The wise should always recite this narrative, which describes the exaltation of devotion and the lives of the devotees, as well as the liberation of Mahendra and the victory of Indra; and those who hear it on every sacred occasion (parvan) gain control over their senses.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame, a liberator from all sins, a conqueror of enemies, a source of well-being, and a promoter of long life.
Śrī Parīkṣit said: O Brahmin, how did the wicked Vṛtra, whose very nature was characterized by passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas),
come to possess such firm devotion toward the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa?

Devotion to the feet of Mukunda generally does not arise even among the gods, who are composed of pure *sattva*, nor among the sages, whose souls are stainless. The living beings here on earth are as numerous as the particles of dust of this world.
Among them, O best of the twice-born, those humans and others who strive for their own welfare are generally seekers of liberation; yet among those seekers of liberation, only a few indeed attain it—
only one in a thousand may be liberated and succeed.
O great sage, even among millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa with a tranquil mind is extremely rare;
how then did that sinful Vṛtra, the tormentor of all the worlds, [attain such a state]?
In this manner, Kṛṣṇa remained firm-minded in that fierce battle.
O Lord, we have a great doubt regarding this matter and a keen desire to hear about it:
how he, by his prowess in combat, satisfied the thousand-eyed Indra.
The venerable Sūta said: Then the blessed Bādarāyaṇi, having heard the inquiry of the faithful Parīkṣit and having rejoiced at his words, spoke.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King,
listen attentively to this ancient history just as it was heard from the mouth of Dvaipāyana, and also from Nārada and Devala.
O King, there was once a sovereign ruler among the Śūrasenas known as Citraketu, whose earth yielded all desires. He had ten thousand times one thousand wives.

Even though he was a king seeking progeny, he did not obtain offspring through them; for although he was endowed with all virtues— beauty, generosity, youth, noble birth, learning, sovereignty, prosperity, and the like— the anxiety of that husband of barren wives remained unfulfilled.
Neither all his riches, nor his beautiful-eyed queens,
nor this earth belonging to him as a sovereign emperor were causes of pleasure for him.
Once, however, the venerable sage Aṅgiras came to his palace.
While wandering through these worlds, he arrived there by chance.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites with rising from his seat, offering salutations, and other such gestures,
and having been received as a guest, he sat down composedly before him once he was comfortably seated.
O great king, the great sage, having honored him who was seated nearby and bowed down with humility upon the ground, addressed him and spoke as follows. Aṅgiras said:

"Is it well with you, and is there welfare for your subjects as well as for yourself, just as a man and a king are protected by their seven constituent elements? By truly establishing oneself within these constituent elements, one attains the highest good."
In that manner, the subjects, the ministers who served the god among men,
his wives, children, counselors, servants, guilds, and ministers, as well as the citizens, the country folk, the vassal kings, and his own sons, were all under his control.
If one’s own self were under one's own control,
then all these worlds, along with their guardians, would offer tribute to him untiringly. Yet the self does not find pleasure in itself, whether through another or by its own power.

"I perceive that you have not attained your desire, for your face is clouded by anxiety. Thus addressed with discernment by the wise sage, O King, he, desiring offspring, bowed down in humility and spoke to the sage.
Citraketu said:
"O Blessed One, what is not known by you— through austerity, knowledge, and meditative absorption—
to those yogis whose sins have been destroyed and who perceive both the external and internal within embodied beings?"
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, since you ask, I shall speak of what has been reflected upon by me;
for though you are already wise, I am impelled to speak by your command.
Even the sovereign powers and riches of empire, which are sought after even by the guardians of the worlds, [are not my goal].
Just as other things do not delight one who is hungry and thirsty, so these do not gladden me, who am childless.
Therefore, O illustrious one, protect me from the darkness that has overtaken me along with my ancestors;
ordain for us that by which we may cross over this difficult-to-traverse state through progeny.
Śrī Śuka said: Thus entreated by Brahmā, the compassionate and omnipresent Lord, the son of Brahmā,
cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru) for Tvaṣṭṛ and performed a sacrifice to him.
O descendant of Bharata, the twice-born sage gave the remnants of the sacrifice to the king’s chief and most excellent queen, who was named Kṛtadyuti.
Then, O King, he said to the monarch: "A single son shall be born to you."
Saying, "You are the one who bestows both joy and sorrow upon me," the son of Brahmā departed;
and by the mere tasting of that [nectar], Queen Kṛtadyuti conceived a child from Citraketu, just as the goddess Kṛttikā conceived Agni as her son.
O King, day by day her embryo grew like the moon in the bright fortnight through the splendor of the Lord of Śūrasena, gradually increasing; then,
when the time had arrived, a son was born.
Producing supreme joy among the Śūrasenas as they listened,
the delighted king— having bathed, purified himself, and adorned himself—
had the brahmins recite benedictions and performed the birth ceremony for the prince.
To them he gave gold, silver, garments, and ornaments;
he bestowed villages, horses, and elephants, as well as six hundred million cows.
To others, he rained down their desired objects, just as the rain-cloud showers upon all embodied beings.
The high-minded [Vasudeva] performed rites that were auspicious, conducive to fame, and life-prolonging for the boy.

Then, as days passed, the father’s affection for his son— who had been obtained with such great difficulty by the royal sage— increased daily, just like the attachment of a poor man toward wealth acquired with hardship.
A mother’s affection for her son is exceedingly great, arising from delusion;
yet in Kṛtadyuti, a fever of longing for offspring arose toward her co-wives,
just as Citraketu felt excessive love for his wife who possessed children.
The affection that arose for the child as he was cherished day after day by them was not felt toward others in such a way.
They tormented themselves, reproaching themselves with envy due to their sorrow over being childless and because of the king’s disregard for them.
"Fie on this sinful woman who is childless and not esteemed as a housewife by her husband,
and who is treated like a slave-girl by her co-wives who have good children!
What grief indeed can there be for slave-girls, since their duty is the service of their master?"
For those who constantly received honors while she, like a wretched slave-girl, was a mere servant,
and for those whose conduct was disapproved by the king, there arose a powerful hatred toward their co-wife on account of her abundance of sons.
Their minds destroyed by hatred, cruel-hearted and intolerant toward the king, the women gave poison to the prince.
Kṛtadyuti, unaware of the great wickedness of her co-wives, [did not intervene].
Thinking, "He is surely asleep," and looking about the house for a long time, the wise woman, having ascertained that the child was lying there, urged her nurse: "O blessed one, bring my son to me."
Approaching him as he lay there and seeing his eyes wide open, yet abandoned by his vital breaths, senses, and self, she cried out, "I am ruined! and fell to the ground.
Hearing the loud, agonized sound of her beating her chest with both hands, [the Lord spoke].

Entering in haste to her son’s side, the queen suddenly beheld her infant son dead; overcome by intense grief, she fell to the ground and fainted, her hair and garments disheveled. Then, hearing the wailing, the people residing in the king’s inner apartments—both men and women—rushed forward.
Having arrived, those women, who shared his misfortune and were deeply distressed, wept piteously as they felt guilty for their transgression.

Hearing that their son was dead—him whose end had been unobserved—the king, his vision destroyed, stumbled and fell along the path; consumed by grief intensified by the bonds of affection, he fainted violently, surrounded by his ministers and brahmins.
He fell at the feet of the dead child, his hair and garments disheveled;
sighing deeply, his throat choked by the obstruction of tears, he was unable to speak. Then, beholding his husband overwhelmed with great grief and his only son, the child, lying dead, he [fainted].
The queen, the virtuous one, who bore the heartache of her subjects and of the state, lamented in many ways; drenching her two breasts adorned with saffron paste with teardrops mixed with collyrium,
and scattering her hair from which the garlands were falling, she mourned for her son with a plaintive cry like that of a female osprey.

"O Creator, you are truly childish, for you strive to produce that which is inconsistent with your own creation! If one being lives while another dies, then you yourself must certainly be subject to death;
for if there were no succession of birth and death here for embodied beings, let it be according to their own past actions."

O Father, this bond of affection which you yourself created for the sake of increasing your own progeny—you now seek to sever it. You ought not to abandon me, wretched and protectorless; look upon your father, who is consumed by grief.
May we easily cross over that darkness which is difficult for the ignorant to traverse; do not go far away with the pitiless Yama.
Arise, dear one! Here are your children and your friends.
"O prince, they call upon you to take your meal;
for you have slept long and are overcome by hunger.
Eat, drink from the breast, and remove the grief of us, your own kin."
"O son, I, whose auspiciousness has been destroyed by you, did not see your lotus-like face with its charming smile and joyful gaze;
or have you gone to another world from which there is no return?"
"Led away by that merciless one, I do not hear even a fraction of your words.
Śrī Śuka said:
[This was spoken] while she lamented with various expressions of grief for her deceased son.
Citraketu, deeply tormented, wept aloud with a broken voice.
As that couple lamented, all their followers—both men and women—wept as well; everything became devoid of consciousness.
Knowing him thus fallen into dejection, deprived of consciousness, and leaderless,
the sage named Aṅgiras arrived along with Nārada.
Śrī Śuka said:
The two of them spoke to the king, who lay prostrate beside the corpse like one dead himself, overwhelmed by grief, awakening him with well-spoken words:
"O Indra among kings, who might this person be whom you lament?"
And what part of this creation are you— formerly, now, or hereafter? Just as grains of sand are carried away by the force of a current,
so do embodied beings, through the power of time, come together and are separated.
Just as seeds within chaff may or may not exist,
so too do living beings within other beings appear through the illusory power (māyā) of the Lord.
Both I and you, as well as these moving and non-moving entities, are of equal duration in time.
O sir, as birth and death do not exist before or after [the creation], so they do not exist even now;
for the Lord of beings creates, sustains, and destroys beings through beings created by Himself,
which are dependent and not independent, though He Himself remains indifferent like a child.

O King, from the body of the embodied one, a new body is born from the [previous] body, just as a seed is produced from a seed; thus the eternal embodied self appears like a distinct object. This distinction between the body and the embodied self was previously created by a lack of discrimination.
"Just as this distinction between genus and individual is imagined with respect to an object," Śrī Śuka said:
"Thus consoled by the words of the twice-born, King Citraketu— "
Wiping his face with his hand, which was withered by distress, he spoke.
Śrī Rājā said:
"Who are you two, endowed with knowledge and the greatest among the great?"
In the guise of ascetics, these two have arrived here in secret;
for those Brahmins who are dear to the Blessed Lord wander at will upon this earth,
appearing as madmen to awaken those like me whose intellects are worldly.
Kumāra, Nārada, Ṛbhu, Aṅgiras, Devala, Asita,
Apāntaratamas, Vyāsa, Mārkaṇḍeya, Gautama,
the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, Kapila, and Bādarāyaṇi.
Durvāsas, Yājñavalkya, Jātukarṇa, and likewise Āruṇi; Romaśa, Cyavana, Datta, Āsuri, along with Patañjali; the sage Vedaśiras, Dhaumya, and the muni Pañcaśikha.
Hiraṇyanābha of Kośala, Śrutadeva, and Ṛtadhvaja—
these and other lords among the perfected ones wander about as causes for the attainment of knowledge.
Therefore, you two are the masters of me, a beast of the village with a deluded intellect.
"Let the lamp of knowledge be raised for one submerged in blind darkness.
Śrī Aṅgiras said:
"O King, I am Aṅgiras, the giver of sons to you who desire a son."
This is the venerable sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā himself; thus,
remembering that you— who are unworthy of such a state— have been submerged in the insurmountable darkness of grief for your son, he has brought to mind the realm of the Great Person.
"O Lord, we two have come here for the sake of bestowing grace upon you.
You, who are devoted to the Brahmanas and a devotee of the Blessed Lord, ought not to disregard us.
At that very moment, having arrived at your home, I shall grant you supreme knowledge."
"Knowing your attachment to another, I shall give you a son myself. Now, the suffering of those who possess children is being experienced by you alone;
likewise [is the suffering] regarding wives, homes, wealth, and various forms of sovereign prosperity."
Sound and other sense objects are fickle, as are the splendors of sovereignty;
the earth, the kingdom, the army, the treasury, the servants, ministers, and friends—
all these, O Śūrasena, are but givers of grief, delusion, fear, and pain.
Resembling a city of Gandharvas, dreams, illusions, and mental fantasies— these mental constructs, though appearing, do not exist as objective realities;
yet, for one who meditates, various actions arise from the mind through the power of past karma.
For this body of the embodied soul, consisting of material objects, knowledge, and action,
is said to be the source of manifold afflictions and torments for the embodied one.
Therefore, with a composed mind, having reflected upon the destiny of the self—
"Abandon reliance on the reality of duality; enter into tranquility.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O disciplined one, receive from me this secret Upaniṣad of mantras."
Bearing which for seven nights, one shall behold the all-pervading Saṅkarṣaṇa; O King,
by approaching the soles of whose feet Śarva and the other gods of old cast off this twofold delusion.
They immediately attained His incomparable and unsurpassed majesty;
you too shall attain it before long.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Then, O King, the celestial sage, having shown the deceased son of the king to his grieving kinsmen, spoke thus. Śrī Nārada said:
"O individual soul, may you be blessed; behold your mother and your father.
Your friends and kinsmen are greatly tormented by the grief caused by you.
Entering your own body, surrounded by your well-wishers, spend the remainder of your life."
"Enjoy the pleasures bestowed by your ancestors and occupy the royal throne.
The Jīva said:
"In which birth did these become my fathers and mothers?"
For one who is wandering through the wombs of gods, animals, and humans by means of their past actions, all beings—
whether relatives, kinsmen, enemies, neutrals, friends, indifferent parties, or foes—
become each other’s counterparts in turn.
Just as commodities such as gold and other goods circulate among men from place to place, so does the individual soul pass through various wombs that act as its makers;
for among men, the connection with eternal objects is seen to be impermanent.
For as long as there is a connection with something, so long indeed does the sense of "mine" (mamatva) persist.
Thus, while residing in the womb, the individual soul (jīva)— which is eternal and devoid of egoism—
possesses ownership over that which it perceives for as long as it is perceived.
He is eternal, immutable, and subtle; He is the refuge of all and self-luminous. By means of the qualities of His own *māyā*, the Lord creates the universe from Himself.
Indeed, there is nothing dear to Him, nor anything unpleasant, whether it be one's own kin or a stranger.
The Self is the solitary witness of all cognitions, of the agents, and of both merits and defects;
for the Self does not take on merit, nor defect, nor the fruit of action.
Sitting like one who is indifferent, the Lord perceives both the high and the low.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having spoken thus, the living entity departed; then his kinsmen, filled with wonder, severed the fetters of self-attachment and cast off their grief.

Having carried away the body of their kinsman and performed the appropriate funeral rites, the relatives abandoned their affection— which is so difficult to relinquish— and which brings about grief, delusion, fear,
and pain. There, the women who had killed the child were ashamed, their splendor destroyed by that act of infanticide.

O great king, remembering the words spoken by the twice-born, they performed the vow for the killing of a child as prescribed by the brāhmaṇas on the banks of the Yamunā. Thus, Citraketu’s soul was awakened by the speech of the twice-born.
Having emerged from his home as an elephant from a dark well or from the mud of a lake,
he bathed according to rule in the Kālindī and performed the sacred water-rites;
with his breath controlled through silence, he paid homage to the two sons of Brahmā.
Then, pleased with that devotee who had sought refuge and whose self was disciplined, the blessed Nārada spoke this knowledge to him:
"Oṃ! We meditate upon You, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva."
Salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṅkarṣaṇa;
salutations to Him who is pure consciousness alone, whose form is supreme bliss,
who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, and whose vision of duality has ceased.
Salutations to the one who has cast off the waves of his own power through the very experience of the bliss of the Self;
salutations to the great Hṛṣīkeśa, whose forms are infinite. Salutations to that One who remains unattained by the mind along with speech when they have ceased.

May He who is without name or form, pure consciousness alone, beyond both being and non-being, protect us; to You, that Brahman— in whom this universe exists, from whom it arises, and into whom it dissolves and is born, just as the nature of clay persists in all things made of clay— we offer our salutation.
I bow down to that which is spread within and without like the sky, which neither the mind, the intellect, the senses, nor the vital breaths touch or know; and by whose particles pierced,
these bodies, senses, breaths, minds, and intellects move about in their respective functions.
At other times, it does not appear as such, like unrefined iron; it attains the designation of "seer" only when situated in its proper places.

Om, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great Person, the one of great majesty, the Lord of great opulences, whose pair of lotus feet are cherished by the bud-like lotus hands of the entire assembly of the foremost Sātvatas;
O Supreme Parameṣṭhin, obeisance unto You!
Śrī Śuka said: O Lord, having instructed this knowledge to the devotee who had sought refuge in him, Nārada departed for the abode of Svāyambhuva along with Aṅgiras.
Citraketu, however, retained that knowledge exactly as it was spoken by Nārada for seven nights, subsisting on water alone and remaining deeply composed. Then,
at the end of those seven nights, by means of that knowledge being maintained, he—
O King, he obtained unimpeded sovereignty over the Vidyādharas;
then, after a few days, his mental movement ignited by spiritual knowledge, he went into the presence of the feet of Śeṣa, the God of gods.

He beheld the Lord, white as a lotus stalk, clad in dark blue garments, adorned with a shimmering crown, armlets, a waistband, and bracelets; His face was serene and His eyes were ruddy, and He was surrounded by circles of the masters of the Siddhas.
With all his sins destroyed by that vision, the sage, his inner self healthy and stainless, approached Him.
With his eyes filled with tears of affection and his hair standing on end from joy, he bowed down before the Supreme Person, who is beyond even Ananta and others.
Repeatedly moistening the lotus-throne of the feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown (*uttamaśloka*) with drops of tears born of love,
he was unable for a long time to offer Him praise, as the flow of all his words was completely obstructed by that very love.

Then, having composed his mind through his intellect and having regained his speech, Citraketu— restraining the outward movement of all his senses— spoke this to the Teacher of the World, who is the very embodiment of the Sātvata scriptures:
Citraketu said:
O Unconquered One, You are conquered by the virtuous who possess equanimity and have mastered their own selves;

and they too are conquered by You, who are most compassionate and grant Your very self to those who worship You without selfish desire. Indeed, O Blessed One, Your power manifests as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
The creators of the universe are but portions of Your portions; therein they vainly contend with separate notions of selfhood.

You are that which exists between the smallest atom and the greatest magnitude, devoid of the three qualities (guṇas), and that which is eternal at the beginning and at the end of beings is indeed the same as that which exists in the interval.

This egg-shell of the universe is indeed enveloped by the seven elements, beginning with earth, each ten times greater than the preceding; within it, along with millions upon millions of other eggs, even the individual soul falls like a mote. He who is infinite is that [Brahman]. Those human-beasts, thirsting for sense-objects, worship your manifestations rather than you, the Supreme.
O Lord, their blessings perish along with them, just like a royal family [that has fallen]. Desires directed toward You do not sprout further, just as parched grain seeds do not grow;
for in You, the self of knowledge who is devoid of qualities, the nets of dualities arising from the multitude of qualities [cease].
O Unconquered One, victory was truly yours when You proclaimed the faultless dharma of the Lord’s devotees—

that dharma which those sages who possess nothing and who delight in the Self practice for the sake of liberation; that dharma wherein there is no sense of partiality among men, nor the notions of "I" and "mine," nor "you" and "yours," directed toward anything other than the Divine.
That which is fashioned with a mind of partiality is indeed impure, perishable, and full of unrighteousness.
What security is there for oneself and others, or what benefit is there in a dharma that harms both self and others?
From harming yourself comes your anger, and likewise, from the oppression of others comes unrighteousness.
Your vision does not fail, for by it the path of devotion (*bhāgavata-dharma*) has been declared;
the noble ones, whose minds are free from dualism, worship You among the multitudes of both stationary and moving beings.
Indeed, O Blessed One, nothing is impossible regarding this: that the sight of You brings about the destruction of all sins for human beings.
Even a *pukkaśa* is liberated from *saṃsāra* by hearing Your name but once;
therefore, O Blessed One, now that the impurities of our hearts have been wiped away by Your glance,
how could that which was spoken by the celestial sage [Nārada] on Your behalf be otherwise?

O Infinite One, the entire conduct of people here in this world is known by You, the Self of the universe; what indeed can be reported to the Supreme Guru, who is like the sun compared to fireflies? Salutations to You, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the maintenance, dissolution, and creation of the entire world.
To Him who is the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*) for those of evil yoga whose understanding of the Self is difficult to attain, and by whom,
as He breathes, the creators of the universe breathe,
and by whom, as He perceives, all thoughts are set in motion.
"Salutations be to that Blessed One of a thousand heads, upon whose crown the entire circle of the earth appears like a mustard seed. Śrī Śuka said:
O descendant of Kuru, being thus praised, the infinite Blessed One spoke with affection to Citraketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas. The Blessed One said:
"O King, you have attained perfection through that instruction which was imparted to Nārada and Aṅgiras by me, as well as through my very sight. Indeed,
I am the self of all beings and the source of all beings."
Both the Brahman of sound and the Supreme Brahman are my two eternal bodies.
Having expanded myself throughout the world and having pervaded the world within myself,
both are permeated by me, and both are established in me.
Just as a person in deep sleep perceives the universe within himself,
yet upon waking from that dream thinks he was situated in only one part of it,
so too are the states of waking and the rest merely stations for the individual soul (jīva) within the Self.

Having understood that these are merely manifestations of *māyā*, one should remember the Supreme Witness by whom the sleeping person perceives his own sleep and the bliss of the attributeless Brahman; know Me to be that Self.
For a person who remembers both [the state of sleep and the state of waking],
that knowledge which persists through them and yet transcends them is Brahman, the Supreme.
It is this very [Brahman] which, when forgotten by a person, causes him to perceive his own nature as distinct from Me.
Thereafter, for such a person, there is the cycle of birth from body to body and death after death; even if one attains a human birth in this world, which is the source of knowledge and realization,
he who does not understand the Self shall never attain security.
Reflecting upon the suffering encountered here in this world, as well as the resulting failure to attain the fruits of one's desires,
and likewise the fearlessness found in freedom from such striving, the wise man should desist from all formative volitions (saṅkalpa).
A husband and wife perform their ritual duties for the sake of happiness and liberation from suffering.
From that [state] follows the non-cessation and non-attainment of both suffering and happiness;
having thus understood this reversal experienced by men who pride themselves on their wisdom,
as well as the subtle course of the Self, which is distinct from the three states of existence.
Freed from the objects of the senses seen and heard, and satisfied by his own splendor through knowledge and realization, a person becomes My devotee.
This alone is the goal for men whose intellects are perfected in yoga.
One’s own true purpose must be understood with all one's being as the vision of the Supreme Self alone.
O King, by faithfully and vigilantly holding to these words of mine,
you— endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom— will quickly attain perfection.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus consoled Citraketu, the Lord Hari, the teacher of the world and the soul of the universe, vanished from his sight.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having offered obeisances to that direction from which Ananta had disappeared,
Citraketu, a Vidyādhara who moves through the sky, wandered in the heavens.
With his strength and senses unimpaired,
that great yogi, being praised by sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas,
dwelt for a hundred thousand years in the valleys of the king of mountain ranges, where various supernatural powers are attained through mere resolve.
He took delight with the women of the Vidyādharas, causing them to sing of Hari,
the Lord. Once, while traveling in a radiant celestial chariot given by Viṣṇu, he beheld Giriśa surrounded by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
In the assembly of sages, having embraced the goddess and taken her onto his lap with his arm,
Citraketu laughed loudly in her presence as she listened,
and said: Citraketu said:
This very teacher of the world, the speaker of dharma for all embodied beings,
sat as the chief in the assembly, united with his wife;
he wore matted hair, performed intense austerities, and was the presiding lord of the assembly of those who discourse on Brahman.
Having accepted a woman, he remains there devoid of shame like an ordinary man;
for while ordinary men generally keep a woman in secret,
this observer of great vows keeps one in public.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having heard that, the Lord, whose intellect is unfathomable, smiled and became silent in the assembly, as did the courtiers who followed his lead.
When he, ignorant of His true power, spoke these many improper words,
the Goddess Śrī Pārvatī, filled with anger, spoke to the audacious one who was arrogant about having conquered his own self.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"What is this man now in the world— a teacher, a wielder of the rod, and a lord— who has been insulted by wicked and shameless people like us? Indeed,
neither the lotus-born Brahmā, nor the sons of Brahmā such as Bhṛgu, Nārada, and others, know the true dharma."

"Indeed, neither the youth Kapila nor Manu forbid us from transgressing against Hara, whose pair of lotus feet are meditated upon by them, who is himself the teacher of the universe and the most auspicious of all auspicious things. This Kṣatrabandhu, however, having insulted the wise sages, commands with arrogance; therefore, he must certainly be punished."

This man, arrogant and stiff with pride, does not deserve to approach the soles of the feet of Vaikuṇṭha, which are worshipped by the virtuous. O evil-minded one, therefore go to a most sinful birth as a demon!
"O son, may you not hereafter commit any offense against the great ones.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus cursed, Citraketu descended from his celestial chariot.
O descendant of Bharata, with his head bowed in humility, Citraketu propitiated Satī;
Citraketu said:
"O Mother, I accept your curse upon myself with my joined palms."
Whatever has been declared by the gods for mortals was indeed ordained for him by destiny in the past.
Deluded by ignorance, a living being wanders within this wheel of worldly existence,
experiencing both happiness and misery everywhere and at all times.
Neither oneself nor another can be the creator of pleasure and pain;
it is the ignorant person here who considers himself or even the Supreme Lord to be the creator.
In this flow of the material modes, what indeed is a curse and what is a favor?
What is heaven, or what is hell? What indeed is happiness, or what is suffering? The one Lord alone creates all beings by means of His own *māyā*;
being partless (*niṣkala*), He alone ordains their bondage and liberation, as well as their happiness and suffering.
To Him no one is dear nor hostile, no relative, kinsman, stranger, or own;
for Him who is equanimous everywhere and untainted, there is no attachment to pleasure, much less anger.
Nevertheless, this emanation of His power exists for their happiness or sorrow, for their benefit or harm.
For embodied beings, it serves for their bondage and liberation, and for the cycle of birth and death.
Now, O beautiful lady, I seek to propitiate you so that you may release me from the curse;
whatever improper words I have spoken, O virtuous one, let them be forgiven.
Śrī Śuka said:
O subduer of enemies, having thus propitiated the two lords of the mountains, Citraketu departed in his own celestial chariot while the two of them looked on with smiles.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke these words to Rudrāṇī while the celestial sages, Daityas, Siddhas, and his own attendants were listening. Śrī Rudra said:
O lady of beautiful hips, you have seen the majesty of Hari, whose deeds are wonderful—
the greatness of those high-souled ones who are free from desire and devoted to their servants. Those who are entirely devoted to Nārāyaṇa do not fear anything whatsoever.

Even in heaven, liberation, or hell, those embodied beings who perceive all objects as equal experience pairs of opposites— happiness and suffering, death and birth, and even curse and grace— due to their connection with a body through the play of the Lord.

For a person acting out of lack of discrimination, the conceptualization of qualities and defects within the Self is created as if it were a real distinction, like the difference between objects or like a [fancied] snake in a garland.
However, for men who bear devotion toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, [such distinctions do not exist].
Indeed, there is no one who can be a refuge for knowledge, detachment, or prowess.
Neither I, nor Viriñca, nor Kumāra and Nārada, nor the sages who are sons of Brahmā, nor the lords of the gods—
though we are but infinitesimal portions of his parts— know his purpose, for we consider ourselves to be separate lords rather than perceiving his true nature.
For there is no one dear to Him, nor anyone not dear, whether one's own kin or a stranger;
because He is the Self of all beings, Hari is beloved by all beings.
And this illustrious Citraketu is His dear follower.

Seeing all things with equanimity and being peaceful, I am indeed dear to Acyuta. Therefore, one should not feel astonishment toward those great-souled men who are devotees of the Supreme Person, who are tranquil, and who possess equal vision.
Śrī Śuka said: O King,
having heard these words spoken by the Lord Śiva,
the goddess became tranquil in mind and her wonder vanished.

Thus, being unable to counter the curse of the goddess, the devotee of the Lord accepted it with his head; for this much is the characteristic of a saintly person. He was born from the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire of Tvaṣṭṛ, having entered a demonic womb.

He who was widely known as Vṛtra was endowed with both theoretical and realized knowledge. All this that you asked me concerning the cause of Vṛtra’s birth among the Asuras and his devotion to the Blessed One has been narrated to you.
Having heard this meritorious history of the high-souled Citraketu,
which describes the greatness of the devotees of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from bondage.
He who, having risen at dawn, recites this with faith while restraining his speech, [attains the same].
Remembering Hari through this history, he attains the supreme goal.
Śrī Śuka said:
Pṛśni, the wife of Savitṛ, [gave birth to] Sāvitrī, Vyāhṛti, and Trayī.
O dear one, Siddhi bore to Bhaga the Agnihotra, Paśu, Soma, Cāturmāsya, and the Mahāmakhās; as well as Mahimā, Vibhu, Prabhu,
Āśis, and a daughter of excellent vows named Varārohā.
Dhātṛ, Kuhū, Sinīvālī, Rākā, and likewise Anumati;
in due order, she established the fires of the earth (purīṣya) at evening for the new moon and at morning for the full moon, remaining ever intent upon her ritual duties.
The earth was the wife of Varuṇa, in whom Bhṛgu was born again;
likewise, the great yogi Vālmīki emerged from an anthill,
as did the sages Agastya and Vasiṣṭha from Mitra and Varuṇa.
The two [Aśvins] quickly shed their semen into a jar in the presence of Urvaśī;
Mitra produced Revatī, Utsarga, Ariṣṭa, and Pippala;
and we have heard that Indra begot three sons upon Paulomī.
O dear one, the Lord begot Jayanta, Ṛṣabha as the third,
and Mīḍhuṣa from Kīrti, the wife of the divine Urukrama, who had assumed the illusory form of Vāmana; their sons were Bṛhacchloka, Saubhaga, and others.

We shall later describe the activities, qualities, and powers of that great-souled Kaśyapa, and how he indeed descended into Aditi. Now, I shall proclaim to you the sons of Kaśyapa who were born as Daityas.
There, the illustrious Bhāgavata Prahlāda and Bali himself— these two sons of Diti, honored by the Daityas and Dānavas—
are celebrated as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
Hiraṇyakaśipu’s wife was a Dānavī named Kayādhu, the daughter of Jambha;
she gave birth to four sons:
first Saṃhrāda, then Anuhrāda, Hrāda, and Prahrāda.
His sister, named Siṃhikā, bore Rāhu to Vipracit—
he whose head Hari severed with his discus while he was drinking the nectar.
Saṃhrāda’s wife was Kṛti, from whom Pañcajana was subsequently born.
Hrāda’s wife was Dhamani, who gave birth to Vātāpi and Ilvala;
it was Ilvala who cooked Vātāpi for his guest Agastya.
Anuhrāda’s sons by Sūryā were Bāṣkala and Mahiṣa.
Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, had Bali as his son by Devī.
From him, a hundred sons were born to Aśanā, of whom Bāṇa was the eldest;
his illustrious power shall be described later.
Bāṇa, having propitiated Giriśa, attained the status of a chief among his attendants,
by whose side the Blessed Lord remains even today as the protector of the city.
And the forty-nine Maruts were the sons of Diti.
They all attained identity with Indra even before their offspring were born.
Śrī Rājā said:
O Guru, how did they cast off their innate demonic nature?
"O Brahman, what good indeed has been done by those whom Indra brought to a state of harmony with himself? For these sages here, along with me, have faith [in him].
O Blessed One, you ought to explain this to us for our full understanding."
Śrī Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Viṣṇurāta, which were truthful, concise, and full of meaning, that son of Badarāyaṇa,
who perceives all things, honored them with a composed mind and spoke to Satrāyaṇa.
Śrī Śuka said: O Indra, Diti, whose sons had been slain by Viṣṇu acting as the rear-guard,
burned with anger and blazed with the fire of grief and reflected thus.

"When shall I lie down in peace after having caused the slayer of my brother— that fierce, sinful man who delights in the senses and possesses an unmelting heart— to be destroyed? For even when addressed by the Lord, he remained as one whose consciousness was reduced to that of a worm, excrement, or ashes."
One who harms living beings for their sake knows nothing of his own true interest, since from that [harm] comes hell. For him who desires this world with an arrogant mind,
may there be a son who dries up Indra’s pride, so that indeed my son may prevail.
With this disposition, O King, she repeatedly performed what was pleasing to her husband through service, affection, humility, self-control, supreme devotion, and charming, sweet speech.
Understanding his inner state, she captivated his mind with her smiles and sidelong glances.
Thus, though he was a wise man, he was rendered senseless by that enchanting woman; that he helplessly said "So be it" is not at all surprising in the case of a woman.
In the beginning, Prajāpati, having observed that all beings were solitary,
created a woman from half of his own body, by whom the minds of men are captivated.
O dear one, in this manner was the blessed Kaśyapa served by his wife.
Laughing, supremely delighted, and greeting her with great joy, Śrī Kaśyapa said to Diti:
"Choose a boon, O lady of beautiful thighs; I am pleased with you, O blameless one."
When a husband is well-pleased with his wife, what desire remains unfulfilled and what gain is there in this world?
For the husband alone is remembered as the supreme deity for women;
indeed, Vāsudeva, the Lord of Śrī, is the mental deity of all living beings.
That very Lord is worshipped by men through the symbols of deities conceived as names and forms; and He assumes the form of a husband for women.
Therefore, O slender-waisted one, women who desire their own welfare should be devoted to their husbands.
They worship with undivided devotion the Lord, who is their own self and their husband.
O blessed lady, I, being thus honored by you with such devotion and disposition,
shall fulfill for you that desire which is very difficult even for unchaste women to attain.
Diti said:
"O Brahmin, if you are a granter of boons to me, I choose as my son one who shall slay Indra—
one who is immortal, for by him my two sons have been killed."
Having heard those words, the brahmin became despondent and was deeply distressed:
"Alas! A very great unrighteousness has now befallen me;
alas! I, who delight in wealth and the senses, have been ensnared here by this illusion consisting of women."
With my mind captivated, I am wretched; I shall surely fall into hell.
What transgression is there in a woman here who follows her own nature?
Fie on me, alas, the ignorant one, for I have failed to conquer my senses regarding my own true interest!
Their faces are a festival of autumn lotuses and their speech is nectar for the ears;
yet their hearts are like the edge of a razor—who can know the conduct of women?
Indeed, no one is truly dear to women, who are essentially devoted only to their own self-interest.
For the sake of wealth, they kill or cause to be killed their husband, son, or brother;
yet the word "I give," once promised, must not become false.
Even Indra does not deserve death for that [debt], and therefore this [means] is devised in such a case.
Having reflected thus, O descendant of Kuru, the blessed Kaśyapa, son of Marīci,
spoke somewhat indignantly while censuring himself.
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
"O blessed lady, a son shall be born to you who will be the slayer of Indra and a friend of the gods,
provided that you maintain this vow for one year with unwavering devotion.
Diti said:
"I shall observe the vow, O Brahmin; please tell me what duties I must perform, and which actions, though prohibited here, do not destroy the vow.
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
One should not harm living beings, nor curse, nor speak untruth;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor touch anything inauspicious;
one should not bathe in water, nor become angry, nor converse with wicked people.
She should not wear unwashed clothes, nor ever a garland that has already been worn.
She should not eat the remnants of food, nor the food of Caṇḍālīs, nor food containing meat, nor food brought by a low-caste person (vṛṣala).
She should not drink water seen by a woman in her courses, nor should she drink water from her joined palms.
At the time of the twilight prayers (sandhyā), she should not go outside with remnants of food on her, without having touched water, with her hair untied,
without being honored, with her speech unrestrained, or without being properly covered.
Nor should she go out with unwashed feet, while impure, with wet feet, or with her head toward the north.
She should not lie down on her back, nor with others, nor naked, nor during the two twilights. Wearing clean clothes, always pure, and endowed with all auspicious things,
she should worship the cows, the Brahmins, Śrī, and Acyuta before her morning meal.

She should honor women who have heroic sons with garlands, perfumes, offerings, and ornaments; having honored her husband, she should attend upon him and meditate on him as being present within her womb.
This vow, known as *puṃsavana*, which ensures the birth of a male child, is to be observed for one year without fail.

"If you will carry [the embryo], a son who shall be the slayer of Śakra will be born to you. Having agreed, saying "So be it," O King, the high-minded Diti then conceived a fetus from Kaśyapa and maintained the vow with unwavering discipline.
O giver of honor, Indra, the wise one, having understood the intention of his maternal aunt, attended upon Diti while she remained in her hermitage, serving her with devotion;
he constantly brought from the forest flowers, fruits, roots, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass.
From time to time, she offered him leaves, sprouts, earth,
and water. O King, while she was thus established in her vow, Hari, seeking a flaw in her observance, wandered about like a deceitful deer in the form of a deer.
O King, being devoted to that vow, Indra did not find any lapse in his observances; then he fell into deep anxiety, thinking, "By what means might there be well-being for me here?
Once, at twilight, she was still impure from eating and emaciated by her vows.
Her feet unwashed by water and untouched, she fell asleep, deluded by fate.
Having found that opportunity while her mind was stolen by sleep, Śakra,
the lord of yoga, entered the womb of Diti by means of his yogic power.

With his thunderbolt, he cut the golden-hued embryo into seven pieces while it was crying out; then, as each of those seven pieces cried "Do not weep! again, O King, they all spoke to him with palms joined in reverence as they were being split apart: "O Lord, do not kill us! We are your sons, born from your own body. (BhP 6.18.62–63)

"O Indra, why do you wish to kill us? The Maruts are your brothers. "Do not fear, O brothers; you are mine," said Kauśika, regarding the hosts of Maruts as his own attendants who possess no other devotion.
The embryo of Diti did not die by the compassion of Śrīnivāsa,
even though it was struck many times by the thunderbolt, just as you were by the weapon of Droṇa’s son.
By worshiping the Original Person even once, a person attains equality with Him.

For a year slightly less than that, Hari was worshipped by Diti together with Indra; those fifty gods became the Maruts. Having removed the defect caused by their mother, they were made drinkers of Soma by Hari.
Diti arose and beheld the boys, radiant as fire;
accompanied by Indra, the blameless goddess was filled with joy. Then she said to Indra: "O dear one, [I shall bring forth sons] who will strike fear into the Ādityas."
Desiring offspring, she observed this vow which is so very difficult to perform. How is it that one son conceived by her became seven times seven?
O son, if this is known to you, tell me the truth; do not speak falsely.
Indra said:

"O Mother, having perceived your resolve, I have come into your presence. Having found an opportunity, I—possessing a mind intent on material gain and not seeing the path of dharma—destroyed the fetus."
"My embryo was cut into seven pieces, becoming seven young boys;
yet each of them was also cut into seven parts, and even so they did not die.
Then, having witnessed that supreme wonder, I made a firm resolve."

The perfection of the worship of the Great Person is some incidental byproduct; those who, desiring the propitiation of the Blessed One, do not seek even the highest [reward] are considered skilled in their own true interest.
Having worshiped the God who bestows the Self, my own soul and the Lord of the universe,
what wise man would choose contact with the material modes, even if it were to result in hell? O Great One, this is the wickedness of me, a fool.
"O Mother, you ought to forgive me; by good fortune, the dead fetus has arisen.
Śrī Śuka said:
"Indra, permitted by her who was satisfied with his pure disposition,"
Having bowed to her along with the Maruts, the Lord departed for the celestial realm.
Thus, everything that you asked me has been related to you:
the auspicious birth of the Maruts. What more shall I tell you?
The King said:
O Brahmin, I wish to know that *puṃsavana* vow which was described by you, by means of which Viṣṇu becomes pleased.
Śrī Śuka said:
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a woman, with the permission of her husband,
should begin from the very beginning this vow which fulfills all desires.
Having heard of the birth of the Maruts and having consulted with the brāhmaṇas, she— having bathed, wearing white garments and white ornaments, and adorned with jewelry—
should worship the Blessed One together with Śrī before her morning meal.
Enough of you who are free from all expectations; O You whose desires are fulfilled, let there be obeisance unto You! Obeisance to the Lord of great opulences, the source of all perfections!
Just as You [act] through Your compassion, prosperity, splendor, majesty, and power...

Since you are favored by all the divine qualities of the Lord, you are therefore the Blessed One, the Sovereign. O Consort of Viṣṇu, O Great Illusion, O You who possess the characteristics of the Supreme Person, O Fortunate One, Mother of the World—may you be pleased with me; salutations unto you!

"Oṃ, obeisances unto the Blessed One, the Great Person, the one of great majesty, the Lord of great opulences; together with his great opulences, I offer this oblation. With this mantra, recited day after day, he should perform the ritual services for Viṣṇu—invocation, water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings—and he should also offer twelve oblations of the remaining sacrificial food into the fire.
"Oṃ, obeisances unto the Blessed One, the Great Person, the Lord of great opulences; svāhā!
One who desires all prosperity should daily worship both Śrī and Viṣṇu with devotion, for they are both the bestowers of boons and the sources of all blessings.
One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground with a mind bowed in devotion;
then one should mutter the mantra ten times and thereafter recite the hymn of praise:
"You two are indeed the all-pervading lords of the universe, the supreme cause of the world."
For this subtle primordial nature is the power of Māyā, difficult to transcend;
you alone are its direct sovereign, the Supreme Person. You are all sacrifices, you are the object of worship, you are the ritual action, and you are the enjoyer of the fruit.
This goddess is the manifestation of the modes of nature, while you are the manifester and the enjoyer of those modes.
For you are the Self who dwells within all bodies; Śrī is the body, the senses, and the mind, while the goddess is name and form, and you are their support and the ground of cognition.
"Just as you two, the supreme lords and bestowers of boons upon the three worlds, are so may my great blessings become true, O Lord of Excellent Renown!
Having thus praised the granter of boons, Śrīnivāsa, together with Śrī, [he spoke].
Having removed that [offering], one should offer the *upaharaṇa* (the final oblation), provide water for sipping (*ācamana*), and perform worship.
Then, with a mind bowed down by devotion, one should praise Him with a hymn of praise.
Having smelled the remnants of the sacrifice, one should again worship Hari.
With supreme devotion and a mind fixed on the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), she should approach her husband with various pleasing services; for the husband, being naturally affectionate,
should himself perform all the duties of his wife, whether they be great or small.
If either one of the two spouses performs [the vow], it is as if both have done so;
however, if the wife is unfit, the husband should perform it himself with a concentrated mind.
One who maintains this vow of Viṣṇu should not let it be interrupted in any way whatsoever.
Day after day, established in her vows, she should worship with devotion the brāhmaṇas and women whose husbands are living, using garlands, perfumes, offerings, and ornaments;
and having dismissed the Lord from His own abode, she should first partake of what was offered to Him.
For the sake of self-purification and for the fulfillment of all desires,
one should spend twelve months— a full year— performing this rite of worship;
then, on the final day of the month of Kārttika, the virtuous woman should desist.
When the next day had dawned, the husband, having touched water and worshipped Kṛṣṇa as before,
should offer twelve oblations of milk boiled with rice and mixed with clarified butter,
according to the procedure for the *pākayajña*.
Having received with his head the blessings uttered by the delighted twice-born,
he should bow his head with devotion and eat with their permission,
placing the teacher at the forefront, remaining silent, and accompanied by his kinsmen.
One should give the remainder of the sacrificial porridge to one's wife for the sake of good offspring and great fortune.
By performing this vow of the Lord according to the injunctions, a man obtains his desired object in this world;
and a woman, by adhering to it, obtains beauty, prosperity, progeny, a husband who lives long, fame, and a home.
And a maiden shall find a husband endowed with all auspicious marks; a woman whose husband has died shall attain the state of one whose sins are destroyed;
a woman whose children have died shall have living sons; an unfortunate woman shall become wealthy; an ill-favored woman shall become beautiful; and one who is deformed shall obtain a supreme form.
One who is diseased shall be freed from illness, and one with impaired senses shall possess a body fit for the senses.
By reciting this during auspicious rites, the ancestors and the gods receive infinite satisfaction.

Being gratified, they grant all desires; at the conclusion of the fire-offering, both the consumer of oblations (Agni) and Śrī Hari bestow them, O King. Thus has been narrated to you the great and meritorious birth of the Maruts and the mighty vow of Diti.
